rashi.eng: *strongholds.*  is palliser in O.F. (strongholds) because (?) they are made in the forest by chopping down trees from all around.

notes.309: (tn, Heb): “Midian, Amalek, and the sons of the east would go up, they would go up against him.” The translation assumes that וְעָלוּ (v�’alu) is dittographic (note the following עָלָיו, ’alayv).

notes.313: (tn, Heb): “They left no sustenance in Israel.”
notes.314: (tn): The words “they took away” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

notes.317: (tn, Heb): “To them and to their camels there was no number.”
notes.318: (tn, Heb): “destroy.” The translation “devour” carries through the imagery of a locust plague earlier in this verse.

rashi.heb:
*הם ומקניהם.* 
לרעות את התבואה:
rashi.eng: *They and their cattle.* (Came) to pasture on the grain.

notes.319: (tn, Heb): “the Lord”; the proper name has been replaced by the pronoun (“he”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.
notes.320: (tn, Heb): “a man, a prophet.” Hebrew idiom sometimes puts a generic term before a more specific designation.
notes.321: (tc): Some ancient witnesses read “from the land of Egypt.” מֵאֶרֶץ (me’erets, “from the land [of]”) could have been accidentally omitted by homoioarcton (note the following מִמִּצְרַיִם [mimmitsrayim, “from Egypt”]).

rashi.heb:
*איש נביא.* 
זה הנביא הוא פנחס, ב"סדר עולם" (פרק ב):
rashi.eng: *a prophet.* This prophet was Phinehas [Seder Olam 20].

notes.323: (tn, Heb): “hand” (also a second time later in this verse).

notes.325: (tn, Heb): “you have not listened to my voice.”

notes.326: (tn): The adjective “angelic” is interpretive. The Lord’s angelic messenger is also mentioned in Judg 2:1.
notes.327: (tn, Heb): “Now Gideon his son…” The Hebrew circumstantial clause (note the pattern vav [ו] + subject + predicate) breaks the narrative sequence and indicates that the angel’s arrival coincided with Gideon’s threshing.
notes.329: (sn): Threshing wheat in a winepress. One would normally thresh wheat at the threshing floor outside the city. Animals and a threshing sledge would be employed. Because of the Midianite threat, Gideon was forced to thresh with a stick in a winepress inside the city. For further discussion see O. Borowski, Agriculture in Iron Age Israel, 63.

rashi.heb:
*אבי העזרי.* 
מבני אביעזר בן גלעד בן מנשה:
rashi.eng: *the Abiezrite.* From the family of Abiezer, of the family of Gilead, of the family of Menasseh.

rashi.heb:
*וגדעון בנו.* 
אביו היה חובטן והוא כוברן, אמר לו: אבא, זקן אתה ואם יבאו המדינים לא תוכל לנוס, לך אתה ואני אחבט:
rashi.eng: *and his son Gideon.* His father was beating them out (i.e., the wheat), and he was sifting them. He then said, “Father, you are old, and if the heathens come, you will not be able to flee. Therefore you go and I will beat them out.”

rashi.heb:
*בגת.* 
בקורות בית הבד:
rashi.eng: *in the winepress.* (he beat the wheat) with the beams of an olivepress (בֵּית הַבַּד).

rashi.heb:
*ה' עמך גבור החיל.* 
שנתן לך כח כזה:
rashi.eng: *The Lord is with you, mighty man of valor.* Since he has granted you such strength.

rashi.heb:
*ויש ה' עמנו.* 
ואם יש ה' עמנו, למה מצאתנו וגו':
rashi.eng: *if the Lord be with us.* (… וְיֵשׁ is to be interpreted as) If God is with us, why has… befallen us?

rashi.heb:
*אשר ספרו לנו אבותינו.* 
פסח היה, אמר לו: אמש הקרני אבא את ההלל, ושמעתיו שהיה אומר (תהלים קיד א): בצאת ישראל ממצרים, 'ועתה נטשנו', אם צדיקים היו אבותינו, יעשה לנו בזכותם, ואם רשעים היו, כשם שעשה להם נפלאותיו חנם כן יעשה לנו, ואיה כל נפלאותיו:
rashi.eng: *which our forefathers told us.* It was Passover so he said, “Last night my father recited the Hallel and I heard him say, ‘When Israel departed from Egypt, etc.,’ (thus recounting the miracles God performed on behalf of Israel,) but now He has forsaken us. If our forefathers were righteous, let Him perform (wonders) for us in their merit, and if they were wicked, then just as He did for them undeserving wonders, so should He do for us. Where then are all His wonders?”

notes.334: (sn): Some interpreters equate the Lord and the messenger in this story, but they are more likely distinct. In vv. 22-23 the Lord and Gideon continue to carry on a conversation after the messenger has vanished (v. 21).
notes.335: (tn, Heb): “Go in this strength of yours.”

rashi.heb:
*ויפן אליו.* 
הקדוש ברוך הוא בעצמו:
rashi.eng: *And the Lord turned toward him.* (Not the angel, but) the Holy One, Blessed be He, Himself.

rashi.heb:
*בכחך זה.* 
בכח הזכות הזה שלמדת סניגוריא על בני, כך דרש רבי תנחומא (מדרש תנחומא שופטים ד):
rashi.eng: *with this your strength.* With the strength of this merit that you advocated defense for my children. So did Rabbi Tanchuma (Shoftim) explain (this passage).

notes.337: (tn, Heb): “he”; the referent (Gideon) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
notes.338: (tn): Note the switch to אֲדֹנָי (’adonay, “Lord”). Gideon seems aware that he is speaking to someone other than, and superior to, the messenger, whom he addressed as אֲדֹנִי (’adoniy, “my lord”) in v. 13.

rashi.heb:
*הנה אלפי.* 
האלף שאני נמנה בו להיות תחת שר האלף, הוא האלף הדל בכל אלפי מנשה:
rashi.eng: *Behold, my thousand.* Heb. אַלְפִּי. The thousand (אֶלֶף) among whom I am counted to be under a head of a thousand is the lowliest (thousand) among all the thousands of Menasseh.

notes.342: (tn, Heb): “You will strike down Midian as one man.” The idiom “as one man” emphasizes the collective unity of a group (see Judg 20:8, 11). Here it may carry the force, “as if they were just one man.”

notes.343: (tn, Heb): “he”; the referent (Gideon) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
notes.344: (tn, Heb): “If I have found favor in your eyes.”

rashi.heb:
*שאתה.* 
כמו שאתה:
rashi.eng: *שָאַתָּה.* Interpreted as if vocalized שֶׁאַתָּה, with a “segol” (“eh” sound).

notes.346: (tn): The Hebrew text adds “to you,” but this has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.
notes.347: (tn, Heb): “and I will bring out my gift.” The precise nuance of the Hebrew word מִנְחָה (minkhah, “gift”) is uncertain in this context. It may refer to a gift offered as a sign of goodwill or submission. In some cases it is used of a gift offered to appease someone whom the offerer has offended. The word can also carry a sacrificial connotation.

notes.348: (tn, Heb): “a kid from among the goats.”
notes.349: (tn): The words “the food” are not in the Hebrew text (an implied direct object). They are supplied in the translation for clarification and for stylistic reasons.

rashi.heb:
*קמח מצות.* 
למדנו שפסח היה, יום תנופת העומר, לכך נאמר (לקמן ז יג) והנה צליל לחם שעורים מתהפך וגו':
rashi.eng: *unleavened cakes of an ephah of meal.* We see that it was Passover, the day of the waving of the Omer, therefore it was said, (below 7: 13) “And behold, a roasted cake of barley bread tumbled, etc.” וְהַמָּרָק. The broth.

rashi.heb:
*והמרק.* 
והרוטב:
rashi.eng: *and the broth.* The broth.

notes.350: (tn, Heb): “Take the meat…and put [it] on this rock.”

notes.352: (tn, Heb): “extended the tip of the staff which was in his hand and touched the meat and unleavened bread.”

notes.355: (tn, Heb): “Gideon.” The proper name has been replaced by the pronoun (“he”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.
notes.357: (tn): The Hebrew text reads אֲדֹנַי יְהוִה (’adonay y�hvih, “Lord [the same title used in v. 15], Lord”).

rashi.heb:
*אהה.* 
לשון דאגה, כלומר מה תהא עלי:
rashi.eng: *Alas.* אֲהָהּ is an expression of “worry” meaning, “What will become (תְּהֵא) of me.”

rashi.heb:
*כי על כן ראיתי.* 
כי על אשר ראיתי מלאך ה', לכך אני דואג וצועק 'אהה':
rashi.eng: *Because I have seen.* (עַל כֵּן is interpreted as עַל אֲשֶׁר) Because I have seen an angel of the Lord, therefore I worry and cry “Alas.”

notes.358: (tn, Heb): “Peace to you.” For a similar use of this idiom to introduce a reassuring word, see Gen 43:23.

notes.359: (tn, Heb): “The Lord is peace.” Gideon’s name for the altar plays on the Lord’s reassuring words to him, “Peace to you.”

rashi.heb:
*ויקרא לו.* 
גדעון למזבח:
rashi.eng: *and he called it.* I.e., Gideon called the altar.

rashi.heb:
*ה' שלום.* 
ה' הוא שלומנו:
rashi.eng: *the Lord is peace.* The Lord is He Who bestows upon us peace.

notes.360: (tn): Or “Take a bull from your father’s herd, the second one, the one seven years old.” Apparently Gideon would need the bulls to pull down the altar.

rashi.heb:
*פר השור.* 
פר הבחור, שהשור בן יומו קרוי שור:
rashi.eng: *the bullock.* A young bull (פַּר), because a one day old ox (שוֹר) is (also) called an ox.

rashi.heb:
*ופר השני.* 
(תרגום:) ותורא תנינא:
rashi.eng: *And the second bullock.*

rashi.heb:
*שבע שנים.* 
(תרגום:) דאיתפטם שבע שנין לעבודה זרה. שמונה דברים הותרו אותו הלילה: מוקצה, אשרה, ולילה, ובמה וכו', כדאיתא בתמורה (כח ב):
rashi.eng: *seven years.* That was fattened seven years for the idols. Eight transgressions were permitted that night. Gideon offered that which was set aside to be sacrificed for idolatry, he used idolatrous utensils, the offering was at night, it was on a private altar and not in the Sanctuary, he was not a priest, sacred vessels were not used, wood from an Asherah was employed, and an animal that was worshipped was used, as is stated in Temurah 28b.

notes.361: (tn): Possibly “in a row” or “in a layer,” perhaps referring to the arrangement of the stones used in the altar’s construction.

rashi.heb:
*ראש המעוז.* 
ראש הסלע:
rashi.eng: *רֹאשׁ הַמָּעוֹז.* On top of the rock.

notes.364: (tn, Heb): “so he did it at night.”

notes.365: (tn, Heb): “look!” The narrator uses this word to invite his audience/readers to view the scene through the eyes of the men.

notes.368: (tn, Heb): “they inquired and searched.” The synonyms are joined to emphasize the care with which they conducted their inquiry.
notes.369: (tn, Heb): “and said.” Perhaps the plural subject is indefinite. If so, it could be translated, “they were told.”

notes.370: (tn, Heb): “and let him die.” The jussive form with vav after the imperative is best translated as a purpose clause.

notes.371: (tn, Heb): “to all who stood against him.”
notes.374: (sn): Whoever takes up his cause will die by morning. This may be a warning to the crowd that Joash intends to defend his son and to kill anyone who tries to execute Gideon. Then again, it may be a sarcastic statement about Baal’s apparent inability to defend his own honor. Anyone who takes up Baal’s cause may end up dead, perhaps by the same hand that pulled down the pagan god’s altar.
notes.376: (tn, Heb): “for he pulled down his altar.” The subject of the verb, if not Gideon, is indefinite (in which case a passive translation is permissible).

rashi.heb:
*האתם תריבון לבעל.* 
בשביל הבעל:
rashi.eng: *Will you contend.* לַבַּעַל ? [The prefix “lamed” does not mean “to” but] for the Baal.

rashi.heb:
*תושיעון אותו.* 
תנקמו נקמתו, וכן (שמואל א כה לב): והושיעה ידי לי, דדוד בנבל:
rashi.eng: *avenge him.* Will you avenge him? Similarly, (I Sam. 25:33) “And from avenging (וְהשׁעַ) myself with my own hand,” which David said concerning Nabal.

rashi.heb:
*אשר יריב לו.* 
בשבילו:
rashi.eng: *He that will contend.* לוֹ For him.

rashi.heb:
*עד הבקר.* 
עד הבקר המתינו:
rashi.eng: *until morning.* Tarry until morning.

rashi.heb:
*אם אלהים הוא.* 
יריב הוא לעצמו ריבו ונקמתו, וכדי לדחותם עד שיברח גדעון היה אומר כן:
rashi.eng: *if he be a god.* Let him contend and avenge himself: He said this in order to delay them until Gideon escaped.

notes.377: (tn, Heb): “He called him on that day Jerub-Baal.” The name means, at least by popular etymology, “Let Baal fight!”

rashi.heb:
*ירב בו.* 
בגדעון אצל ריב נופל עם, או את, או בו, כמו (בראשית לא לו): וירב בלבן, אבל 'לו' אינו נופל על הלשון, וכל 'לו' הכתובים כאן 'בשביל' הם:
rashi.eng: *contend with him.* i.e., with Gideon. Near (the word) רִיב, the word עִם or אֶת or בּוֹ is used as in, (Gen. 31:36) “And he quarreled with Laban”, but לוֹ cannot be used with this expression. Hence, every לוֹ written here means “for (him)”.

notes.378: (tn, Heb): “Midian, Amalek, and the sons of the east.”
notes.379: (tn): The words “the Jordan River” are not in the Hebrew text, but are supplied in the translation for clarification.

rashi.heb:
*רוח ה'.* 
רוח גבורה:
rashi.eng: *And a spirit of the Lord.* A spirit of might.

rashi.heb:
*ויזעק אביעזר.* 
כל המשפחה:
rashi.eng: *and Abiezer gathered.* I.e., the entire family.

notes.383: (tn, Heb): “and he also was summoned after him.”

notes.384: (tn): More literally, “you are about to deliver Israel by my hand.”
notes.385: (tn): The words “then give me a sign as proof” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

notes.388: (tn, Heb): “you will deliver Israel by my hand.”

notes.390: (tn, Heb): “dew dripped from the fleece – a bowl full of water.”

rashi.heb:
*ויהי כן.* 
שהיה טל על הגזה לבדה יותר מבשאר מקומות, כמו שהוא אומר (פסוק לז): מלא הספל מים, אבל 'על כל הארץ חורב' לא נתקיים, שהברית כרותה לטל שאינו נעצר (תענית ג א):
rashi.eng: *And it was so.* There was only dew on the fleece, more so than on other places, as it says, “A bowl full of water.” However, “Upon all the ground it be dry” was not fulfilled because a covenant was made with the dew that it should not cease.

rashi.heb:
*ויזר.* 
לשון מכבש, וכן (ישעיהו א ו): לא זורו ולא חובשו, לא נחבשו להוציא הלחה:
rashi.eng: *and pressed.*  An expression of “pressed,” and similarly, (Isa. 1:6) “They were neither pressed (זוֹרוּ) nor bandaged,” i.e., they were not pressed to extract the pus.

notes.391: (tn, Heb): “Let your anger not rage at me, so that I might speak only this once.”
notes.392: (tn, Heb): “let the fleece alone be dry, while dew is on all the ground.”

notes.394: (tn, Heb): “and all the people who were with him.”
notes.396: (tn, Heb): “Midian.” The LXX reads “and Amalek” (cf. v. 12; 6:33).

rashi.heb:
*מגבעת המורה בעמק.* 
(תרגום:) דמסתכיא למישרא. המורה, לשון הוראה וראיה, כמו (משלי ו יג) מורה באצבעותיו, שמשם צופים ורומזים בעמק:
rashi.eng: *By Gibeath moreh, in the valley.* (מִגִּבְעַת הַמּוֹרָה בָּעֵמֶק.) by the mountain that overlooks the plain (Targum Jonathan). הַמּוֹרָה is an expression of instructing and looking (וּרְאִיָּה הוֹרָאָה, as in (Prov. 6:13) “Instructing (מוֹרֶה) with his fingers,” because from there, one could see and signal into the valley.

notes.397: (tn, Heb): “the people who are with you are too numerous for me to give Midian into their hand.”

rashi.heb:
*יתפאר.* 
וונטי"ר בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *vaunt.* vanter in French (i.e., praise themselves)

notes.400: (tn, Heb): “call into the ears of the people.”
notes.402: (tc): Many interpreters reject the MT reading “and leave Mount Gilead” for geographical reasons. A possible alternative, involving rather radical emendation of the Hebrew text, would be, “So Gideon tested them” (i.e., thinned the ranks in this manner).
notes.403: (tn, Heb): “people.” The translation uses “men” because warriors are in view, and in ancient Israelite culture these would be only males. (This is also the case in vv. 4, 5, 6, 7, 8.)

rashi.heb:
*ויצפר.* 
בבקר, לשון ארמי: צפרא:
rashi.eng: *and depart early.* Heb. וְיִצְפֹּר. I.e., in the morning, as in the Aramaic term צַפְרָא (morning).

notes.411: (tn, Heb): “Everyone who laps with his tongue from the water, as a dog laps, put him by himself, as well as the one who gets down on his knees to drink.”

rashi.heb:
*כל אשר ילוק בלשונו וגו' וכל אשר יכרע על ברכיו לשתות.* 
תציג אותו לבד חוץ מסיעתך, כי הם לא ילכו עמך, שכך הם למודים לכרוע לפני עבודת גלולים:
rashi.eng: *“Every one who laps with his tongue, etc., and (likewise) every one that kneels upon his knees to drink.”.* Set him (i.e., he who kneels) separately away from your group because they will not go with you since they are thus accustomed to kneel before idols.

notes.412: (tc): The Hebrew text adds, “with their hands to their mouths,” This makes no sense in light of v. 5, which distinguishes between dog-like lappers (who would not use their hands to drink) and those who kneel (who would use their hands). It seems likely that the words “with their hands to their mouths” have been misplaced from v. 6. They fit better at the end of v. 5 or v. 6. Perhaps these words were originally a marginal scribal note which was later accidentally inserted into the text in the wrong place.

rashi.heb:
*המלקקים בידם.* 
אין זה דרך כריעה כלוקק בלשונו:
rashi.eng: *of those that lapped, putting their hand….* This is not a kneeling procedure just as one who laps with his tongue (is not considered kneeling).

notes.414: (tn, Heb): “you.” The Hebrew pronoun is masculine plural, probably referring to the entire army.
notes.415: (tn): The Hebrew pronoun here is singular.
notes.416: (tn, Heb): “All the people should go, each to his place.”

notes.418: (tn): The words “who were chosen” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
notes.419: (tn): The Hebrew text has “in their hands.”
notes.420: (tn, Heb): “he”; the referent (Gideon) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

notes.424: (tn, Heb): “him”; the referent (Gideon) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
notes.426: (tn): The Hebrew verbal form is a perfect, emphasizing the certainty of the promise.

notes.428: (tn, Heb): “to the edge of the ones in battle array who were in the camp.”

notes.429: (tn, Heb): “Midian, Amalek, and the sons of the east were falling in the valley like locusts in great number.”

rashi.heb:
*נפלים בעמק.* 
שוכנים בעמק:
rashi.eng: *נֹפְלִים בָּעֵמֶק.* I.e., they were encamped in the valley.

notes.430: (tn, Heb): “And Gideon came, and, look, a man was relating to his friend a dream.”
notes.431: (tn, Heb): “he”; the referent (the man mentioned in the previous clause) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
notes.432: (tn, Heb): “Look!” The repetition of this interjection, while emphatic in Hebrew, would be redundant in the English translation.
notes.433: (tn, Heb): “It came to the tent and struck it and it fell. It turned it upside down and the tent fell.”

rashi.heb:
*צליל ; צלול' כתיב, שהיה הדור צלול מן הצדיקים: צליל לחם שערים.* 
(תרגום:) חרר דלחם שעורים, חררה שאופין על הגחלים:
rashi.eng: *צְלִיל.* This is written צְלִול (i.e., empty), because the generation was empty of righteous people. צְלִיל לֶחֶם שׂעוֹרִים A roasted barley bread (Targum Jonathan). A cake baked (צְלִי) on coals.

rashi.heb:
*לחם שערים.* 
הוא זכות העומר הקרב בפסח:
rashi.eng: *barley bread.* Symbolizing the merit of the Omer sacrificed on Passover.

rashi.heb:
*ויכהו ויפל.* 
האהל:
rashi.eng: *and smote it, and it fell.* i.e., The tent.

rashi.heb:
*ויהפכהו.* 
האהל מלמטה למעלה, ונפל האהל:
rashi.eng: *and it turned it.* i.e., The tent was completely overturned, and fell.

rashi.heb:
*את מספר החלום.* 
את סיפור החלום, (תרגום:) ית שועית חלמא וית פשריה:
rashi.eng: *telling of the dream.* Heb. מִסְפַּר). The story (סִפּוּר) of the dream, (as Targum Jonathan renders) יַת שוּעִית חֶלְמָא וְיַת פִּשְׁרֵיהּ (the telling of the dream and its interpretation).

rashi.heb:
*ואת שברו.* 
ואת ממכרו, כלומר: ואת פתרונו:
rashi.eng: *and its interpretation.* Its exchange; meaning, its interpretation (which takes the place of the dream).

notes.438: (tn, Heb): “the jars.” The noun has been replaced by the pronoun (“them”) in the translation for stylistic reasons. They hid the torches inside the earthenware jars to disguise their approach and to keep the torches from being extinguished by the breeze.

rashi.heb:
*שופרות ולפדים.* 
להזכיר זכות מתן תורה ופשוטו: לילה היה, כמו שכתוב (פסוק ט) והיה חשך, לפיכך נשאו שם לפידים להאיר להם ונתנום בכדים כדי שלא יבינו בלפידים:
rashi.eng: *trumpets… torches.* To commemorate the merit of the giving of the Torah. However, the simple meaning is that since it was night, as it states (v. 9), it was dark, therefore they took the torches to provide light, and placed them into pitchers lest the torches be discerned.

rashi.heb:
*ממני תראו.* 
את אשר אני עושה, ראו ועשו כן:
rashi.eng: *You shall look at me.* At what I do, and do likewise.

rashi.heb:
*אנכי וכל אשר אתי.* 
אחד מן הראשים, ומאה איש היה עמו (פסוק ט):
rashi.eng: *I and all that are with me.* One of the companies consisting of one hundred men was with him.

rashi.heb:
*לה' ולגדעון.* 
(תרגום:) חרבא דמקטלא מן קדם ה' ונצחנא על ידי גדעון:
rashi.eng: *For the Lord and for Gideon.* (Targum Jonathan paraphrases:) The sword that kills is prompted by the Lord, and the victory is through Gideon.

notes.440: (tn, Heb): “Gideon went, along with the hundred men who were with him, to the edge of the camp.”

rashi.heb:
*הקם הקימו.* 
כבר בני החיל את השומרים שהיתה משמרתם באשמורת התיכונה, שכן דרך בני גייסות להעמיד שומרים, אלו ישמרו שליש הלילה הראשון ואלו שליש השני, ואלו שליש האחרון:
rashi.eng: *they had but recently awakened.* I.e., The soldiers previously (had but recently awakened) the guards, who were to guard during the middle watch; for so it is customary for soldiers to set up watchmen, these would watch for the first third of the night, these for the second third, and these for the last third.

rashi.heb:
*ונפוץ הכדים.* 
ולשבור הכדים אשר בידם:
rashi.eng: *and they smashed the pitchers that were in their hands.* (and he told them) to break the pitchers which were in their hands.

notes.442: (tn): The Hebrew text adds, “in order to blow [them].” This has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.

rashi.heb:
*ויריעו.* 
תרועת מסע וניסה:
rashi.eng: *and they trumpeted.* A blast to disencamp and flee.

notes.445: (tn, Heb): “the Lord set the sword of each one against his friend.”
notes.446: (tc): MT has “and throughout the camp,” but the conjunction (“and”) is due to dittography and should be dropped. Compare the ancient versions, which lack the conjunction here.
notes.447: (tn): The words “they went” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

notes.451: (tn): The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for clarification (also later in this verse).
notes.452: (tn, Heb): “And all the men of Ephraim were summoned.”

rashi.heb:
*ולכדו להם את המים.* 
המפסיקין בין ארם לארץ כנען:
rashi.eng: *and seize before them the waters.* Which separate between Edom and Canaan (Text per Rabbi Joseph Karo).

rashi.heb:
*ואת הירדן.* 
שגם הוא היה מפסיק:
rashi.eng: *and (also) the Jordan.* For it also separated.

notes.454: (sn): The names Oreb and Zeeb, which mean “Raven” and “Wolf” respectively, are appropriate because the Midianites had been like scavengers and predators to Israel.
notes.455: (tn): The Hebrew text repeats the verb “executed.” This has not been repeated in the translation for stylistic reasons.
notes.457: (tn, Heb): “beyond the Jordan.” The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text but has been supplied in the translation for clarity (also in 8:4).

rashi.heb:
*הביאו אל גדעון מעבר לירדן.* 
בבקר, כשעבר גדעון את הירדן לרדוף אחר זבח וצלמונע:
rashi.eng: *they brought to Gideon beyond the Jordan.* In the morning, when Gideon crossed the Jordan in pursuit of Zebah and Zalmunna.

notes.460: (sn): Ephraim’s leftover grapes are better quality than Abiezer’s harvest. Gideon employs an agricultural metaphor. He argues that Ephraim’s mopping up operations, though seemingly like the inferior grapes which are missed initially by the harvesters or left for the poor, are actually more noteworthy than the military efforts of Gideon’s family.

rashi.heb:
*מה עשיתי עתה ככם.* 
מה חשוב מה שעשיתי בתחילתו, כמה שעשיתם אתם בסוף:
rashi.eng: *What have I done now in comparison with you?.* Of what importance is what I did at first, compared with what you subsequently did.

rashi.heb:
*הלא טוב עללות.* 
שבאו לידכם בסוף מתחלת הבציר שבצרנו אני ומשפחתי, שהרי בידכם נתן ה' את המלכים:
rashi.eng: *Are not the gleanings… better.* Are not the gleanings that came to your hand at the end better than the vintage that I and my family picked in the beginning, considering that in your hands the Lord delivered the kings (i. e., the princes).

notes.461: (tn, Heb): “What was I able to do compared to you?”
notes.462: (tn, Heb): “Then their spirits relaxed from against him, when he spoke this word.”

rashi.heb:
*ומה יכלתי.* 
לעשות שיהא חשוב כמעשה שלכם:
rashi.eng: *and what was I able.* to do that would be as outstanding as your deed?

notes.463: (tn, Heb): “And Gideon arrived at the Jordan, crossing over, he and the three hundred men who were with him, exhausted and chasing.” The English past perfect (“had crossed”) is used because this verse flashes back chronologically to an event that preceded the hostile encounter described in vv. 1-3. (Note that 7:25 assumes Gideon had already crossed the Jordan.)

rashi.heb:
*עבר הוא ושלש מאות האיש.* 
עוברים את הירדן אחרי זבח וצלמונע שעברו את הירדן תחלה, והיו משחיתים מעבר לירדן את ארץ ראובן וגד ומנשה, ועבר שם כדי לנקום אף בהם:
rashi.eng: *he crossed, and the three hundred men.* They were crossing the Jordan after Zebah and Zalmunna who had passed earlier (perhaps even prior to the blockade above 7:24) and laid waste to the land of Reuben, Gad and Menasseh. Therefore, he crossed to take revenge against them also.

notes.465: (tn, Heb): “people.” The translation uses “men” because these were warriors and in ancient Israelite culture would have been exclusively males.

rashi.heb:
*לאנשי סכות.* 
ישראל היו:
rashi.eng: *to the men of Succoth.* Who were Israelites.

notes.468: (tn, Heb): “Are the palms of Zebah and Zalmunna now in your hand, that we should give to your army bread?” Perhaps the reference to the kings’ “palms” should be taken literally. The officials of Succoth may be alluding to the practice of mutilating prisoners or enemy corpses (see R. G. Boling, Judges [AB], 155). The officials of Succoth are hesitant to give (or sell) food to Gideon’s forces because they are not sure of the outcome of the battle. Perhaps they had made an alliance with the Midianites which demanded their loyalty.

rashi.heb:
*הכף זבח וצלמנע בידך.* 
שאתה מתפאר שהצלתנו מיד מדין:
rashi.eng: *Is the palm of Zebah and Zalmunna now in your hand.* That you boast that you saved us from Midian?

notes.470: (sn): I will thresh. The metaphor is agricultural. Threshing was usually done on a hard threshing floor. As farm animals walked over the stalks, pulling behind them a board embedded with sharp stones, the stalks and grain would be separated. See O. Borowski, Agriculture in Iron Age Israel, 63-65. Gideon threatens to use thorns and briers on his sledge.
notes.472: (tn): This is apparently a rare instrumental use of the Hebrew preposition אֵת (’et, note the use of ב [bet] in v. 16). Some, however, argue that אֵת more naturally indicates accompaniment (“together with”). In this case Gideon envisions threshing their skin along with thorns and briers, just as the stalks and grain are intermingled on the threshing floor. See C. F. Burney, Judges, 229-30.

rashi.heb:
*הברקנים.* 
רונצי"ש בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *the briers.* Ronzes in O.F.

notes.473: (tn, Heb): “and spoke to them in the same way.”
notes.474: (tn, Heb): “The men of Penuel answered him just as the men of Succoth answered.”

notes.475: (tn, Heb): “said to.” The translation “threatened” is interpretive, but is clearly indicated by the context.

notes.478: (tn, Heb): “About fifteen thousand [in number] were all the ones remaining from the army of the sons of the east. The fallen ones were a hundred and twenty thousand [in number], men drawing the sword.”

rashi.heb:
*בקרקר.* 
שם מקום:
rashi.eng: *were in Karkor.* The name of a place.

notes.480: (tn, Heb): “and attacked the army, while the army was secure.” The Hebrew term בֶטַח (vetakh, “secure”) probably means the army was undefended (see R. G. Boling, Judges [AB], 156), not suspecting an attack at that time and place.

rashi.heb:
*דרך השכוני באהלים.* 
דרך ארץ קדר וערב השוכנים במדבר באהליהם, שרועים מקנה תמיד ואין דרים בבתים:
rashi.eng: *by the way of the tent dwellers.* Through the land of Kedar and Arabia, whose people live in the desert in tents, constantly grazing their flock and not residing in houses.

rashi.heb:
*מקדם לנבח ויגבהה.* 
שהם ערי ישראל, ולא רצה לילך שם אלא דרך עקלתון, כדי שלא ירגישו בהם, ויהומם פתאום:
rashi.eng: *on the east of Nobah and Jogbehah.* Which were Israelite cities. However, he only wanted to go there roundabout, so that they should not be detected, and thereby suddenly surprise them.

notes.481: (tn, Heb): “he”; the referent (Gideon) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

rashi.heb:
*מלמעלה החרס.* 
עד שלא שקעה השמש, בעוד החמה נראית גבוה:
rashi.eng: *when the sun was still high.* I.e., when the sun had not yet set, while the sun (חֶרֶס) still appears high (לְמַעֲלָה).

notes.485: (tn, Heb): “wrote down for him the officials of Succoth and its elders, seventy-seven men.”

notes.486: (tn, Heb): “Look!” The words “what I have” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
notes.487: (tn, Heb): “Are the palms of Zebah and Zalmunna now in your hand, that we should give to your exhausted men bread?” Gideon changes their actual statement (see v. 6) by saying exhausted men rather than “army.” In this way he emphasizes the crisis his men were facing and highlights the insensitivity of the men of Succoth.

notes.489: (tc): The translation follows the reading of several ancient versions (LXX, the Syriac Peshitta, and Vulgate) in assuming the form וַיָּדָשׁ (vayyadash) from the verb דּוֹשׁ (dosh, “thresh”) as in v. 7. The MT reads instead the form וַיֹּדַע (vayyoda’, “make known”), a Hiphil form of יָדַע (yadah). In this case one could translate, “he used them [i.e., the thorns and briers] to teach the men of Succoth a lesson.”

rashi.heb:
*וידע בהם.* 
(תרגום:) ותבר בהון:
rashi.eng: *וַיּוֹדַע בָּהֶם.* And broke with them.

notes.491: (tn, Heb): “each one like the appearance of sons of the king.”

rashi.heb:
*אחד כתאר בני המלך.* 
יונתן תרגם: אחד היה בהם שתוארו כתואר בני המלך. ויש לפותרו: כמוך כמוהם, תואר אחד לכם, כי כתואר בני מלכים היו:
rashi.eng: *One was as the form of the children of the king.* Heb. אֶחָד כְּתֹאַר בְּנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ. Targum Jonathan renders: One among them appeared like the children of the king. However, we can interpret: As you are, so were they, all of you possessing one appearance (כָּמוֹךָ כְמוֹהֶם אֶחָד); since they appeared like the children of kings (כְּתֹאַר בְּנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ).

notes.492: (tn): The words “I swear” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

notes.494: (tn, Heb): “did not draw his sword for he was afraid.”

rashi.heb:
*ולא שלף הנער חרבו.* 
להורגם, שהיה ירא מהם:
rashi.eng: *But the young man did not draw his sword.* To kill them, because he was afraid of them.

notes.495: (tn): The words “to Gideon” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
notes.497: (tn, Heb): “for as the man is his strength.”

rashi.heb:
*השהרנים.* 
לוינ"ש בלע"ז, של זהב:
rashi.eng: *the crescents.* Of gold, lunettes in O.F.

notes.501: (tn, Heb): “Give to me, each one, an earring from his plunder.”
notes.502: (tn, Heb): “they”; the referent (the Midianites) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

notes.504: (tc): In the LXX the subject of this verb is singular, referring to Gideon rather than to the Israelites.

notes.505: (sn): Seventeen hundred gold shekels would be about 42.7 pounds (19.4 kilograms) of gold.
notes.507: (tn, Heb): “the ornaments which were on the necks of their camels.”

rashi.heb:
*השהרנים והנטפות.* 
(תרגום:) ענקיא וכלילא:
rashi.eng: *הַשַּׂהֲרוֹנִים וְהַנְּטִיפוֹת.* The crescents and the pendants [after Targum Jonathan].

notes.509: (sn): In Exod 28:4-6 and several other texts an ephod is described as a priestly or cultic garment. In some cases an ephod is used to obtain a divine oracle (1 Sam 23:9; 30:7). Here the ephod is made of gold and is described as being quite heavy (70-75 lbs?). Some identify it as an idol, but it was more likely a cultic object fashioned in the form of a garment which was used for oracular purposes. For discussion of the ephod in the OT, see C. F. Burney, Judges, 236-43, and R. de Vaux, Ancient Israel, 349-52.
notes.511: (tn): The words “by worshiping it” are supplied in the translation for clarity.

rashi.heb:
*ויעש אותו גדעון לאפוד.* 
להיות לזכרון על תשועה גדולה, לראות כמה היה חילם כבד שבנזמי חשוביהם היה כל הזהב הזה:
rashi.eng: *And Gideon made it into an Ephod.* To serve as a reminder of the great victory, by showing how immense their army was that the nose rings of the nobles amounted to all this gold.

rashi.heb:
*ויזנו כל ישראל אחריו.* 
לאחר מיתת גדעון:
rashi.eng: *and all Israel went astray after it.* After Gideon’s death.

notes.512: (tn, Heb): “Midian was humbled before the Israelites, and they no longer lifted their heads.”

notes.514: (tn, Heb): “went and lived in his house.”

notes.515: (tn, Heb): “Gideon had seventy sons who went out from his thigh, for he had many wives.” The Hebrew word יָרֵךְ (yarekh, “thigh”) is a euphemism here for the penis.

notes.516: (sn): A concubine was a slave woman in ancient Near Eastern societies who was the legal property of her master, but who could have legitimate sexual relations with her master. A concubine’s status was more elevated than a mere servant, but she was not free and did not have the legal rights of a free wife. The children of a concubine could, in some instances, become equal heirs with the children of the free wife. After the period of the Judges concubines may have become more of a royal prerogative (2 Sam 21:10-14; 1 Kgs 11:3).
notes.517: (sn): The name Abimelech means “my father is king.”

notes.519: (sn): Baal-Berith was a local manifestation of the Canaanite storm god. The name means, ironically, “Baal of the covenant.” Israel’s covenant allegiance had indeed shifted.

rashi.heb:
*בעל ברית.* 
כך שמו:
rashi.eng: *Baal- berith.* This was its name.

notes.521: (tn, Heb): “did not do loyalty with,” or “did not act faithfully toward.”

rashi.heb:
*ולא עשו חסד וגו'.* 
שהרגו את בניו, כמו שכתוב בענין (להלן ט ה):
rashi.eng: *And they did not do kindness with the house of Jerubbaal.* They killed his sons, as Scripture states below (9: 5).

notes.523: (tn, Heb): “to all the extended family of the house of the father of his mother.”

notes.525: (tn, Heb): “What good is it to you?”

notes.530: (tn, Heb): “Their heart was inclined after Abimelech.”

rashi.heb:
*ופחזים.* 
בהולים במעשיהם לעשות בלא תבונה:
rashi.eng: *and hasty.* פוֹחֲזִים. Hasty in their actions, to do without meditation.

notes.535: (tn): The word “legitimate” is not in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for clarification.

notes.537: (tc): The translation assumes that the form in the Hebrew text (מֻצָּב, mutsav) is a corruption of an original מַצֵּבָה (matsevah, “pillar”). The reference is probably to a pagan object of worship (cf. LXX).

rashi.heb:
*עם אלון מצב.* 
(תרגום:) מישר קמתא - מישור שהיו בו מצבות:
rashi.eng: *by the plain of the stones.* Heb. אֵלוֹן מֻצָּב. Targum Jonathan renders מֵישַׁר קָמָתָא, i.e., a plain (אֵלוֹן) containing monuments (מַצֵּבוֹת).

notes.538: (tn, Heb): “And they reported to Jotham.” The subject of the plural verb is indefinite.
notes.539: (tn, Heb): “He lifted his voice and called and said to them.”

notes.540: (tn, Heb): “Going they went, the trees.” The precise emphatic force of the infinitive absolute (“Going”) is not entirely clear. Perhaps here it indicates determination, as in Gen 31:30, where one might translate, “You have insisted on going away.”
notes.541: (tn, Heb): “to anoint [with oil] over them a king.”

rashi.heb:
*הלוך הלכו העצים.* 
משל הוא:
rashi.eng: *the trees went forth.* This is allegorical.

rashi.heb:
*לזית.* 
עתניאל בן קנז (שופטים א יג), הבא משבט יהודה שנקרא זית, שנאמר (ירמיהו יא טז): זית רענן יפה פרי תואר וגו':
rashi.eng: *to the olive tree.* Referring to Othniel the son of Kenaz from the tribe of Judah, which is called an olive tree, as it says, (Jer. 11:16) “Like a fresh olive tree, beautiful in form, etc.” (this refers to the cities of Judah mentioned in v. 13 ibid).

notes.543: (tn, Heb): “Should I stop my abundance, with which they honor gods and men, and go to sway over the trees?” The negative sentence in the translation reflects the force of the rhetorical question.

rashi.heb:
*דשני.* 
לשון שומן:
rashi.eng: *דִּשְׁנִי.* This is an expression of “fatness.”

rashi.heb:
*לתאנה.* 
דבורה:
rashi.eng: *to the fig tree.* Deborah.

notes.545: (tn, Heb): “Should I stop my sweetness and my good fruit and go to sway over the trees? The negative sentence in the translation reflects the force of the rhetorical question.

rashi.heb:
*את מתקי.* 
דבש דבורים:
rashi.eng: *my sweetness.* (Referring to) the bee’s honey.

rashi.heb:
*לגפן.* 
גדעון, שהוא מזרע יוסף (שופטים ו יא), שנאמר בו (בראשית מט כב) בן פורת, (ותרגם שם אונקלוס:) כגופן דנציב וכו':
rashi.eng: *to the vine.* Referring to Gideon who descended from Joseph of whom it is said, (Gen. 49:22) “A fruitful son is Joseph; blessed as a vine standing by the water” (as per Onkelos).

notes.547: (tn, Heb): “Should I stop my wine, which makes happy gods and men, and go to sway over the trees?” The negative sentence in the translation reflects the force of the rhetorical question.

rashi.heb:
*המשמח אלהים.* 
שאין אומרים הלוים שיר של הקרבן אלא על הנסכים:
rashi.eng: *which causes God… to rejoice.* For the Levites do not recite the sacrificial song of praise but during the libations of wine.

rashi.heb:
*אל האטד.* 
ספינ"ה בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *To the thorn.* Heb. הָאָטָד, epine in O.F.

rashi.heb:
*אם באמת.* 
שאני הגון למלכות:
rashi.eng: *If in truth.* I.e., because I am fit to rule.

notes.553: (tn, Heb): “if according to the deeds of his hands you have done to him.”

notes.554: (tc, Heb): “threw his life out in front,” that is, “exposed himself to danger.” The MT form מִנֶּגֶד (minneged, “from before”) should probably be read as מִנֶּגְדּוֹ (minnegdo, “from before him”); haplography of vav has likely occurred here in the MT.

notes.558: (tn): The word “legitimate” is not in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for clarification.

notes.561: (tn, Heb): “then rejoice in Abimelech, and may he also rejoice in you.”

notes.562: (tn, Heb): “fled and ran away and went.”

notes.565: (tn): The Hebrew verb translated “commanded” (שָׂרַר, sarar), which appears only here in Judges, differs from the ones employed earlier in this chapter (מָשַׁל [mashal] and מָלַךְ [malakh]). Abimelech commanded Israel. Perhaps while ruling as king over the city-state of Shechem, Abimelech also became a leader of the Israelite tribal alliance (see R. G. Boling, Judges [AB], 175).

rashi.heb:
*וישר.* 
על כרחם נהג רבנות ובגאוה:
rashi.eng: *And Abimelech ruled.* Forcefully and arrogantly he held his position.

notes.566: (tn, Heb): “an evil spirit.” A nonphysical, spirit being is in view, like the one who volunteered to deceive Ahab (1 Kgs 22:21). The traditional translation, “evil spirit,” implies the being is inherently wicked, perhaps even demonic, but this is not necessarily the case. The Hebrew adjective רָעַה (ra’ah) can have a nonethical sense, “harmful; dangerous; calamitous.” When modifying רוּחַ (ruakh, “spirit”) it may simply indicate that the being in view causes harm to the object of God’s judgment. G. F. Moore (Judges [ICC], 253) here refers to a “mischief-making spirit.”
notes.567: (tn, Heb): “The leaders of Shechem were disloyal.” The words “he made” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

rashi.heb:
*רוח רעה.* 
שנאה, שלנ"ש מלטלינ"ט בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *an evil spirit.* A spirit of hatred, (טלנט), talent in O.F.

notes.569: (tn, Heb): “so that the violence done to the seventy sons of Jerub-Baal might come, and their blood might be placed on Abimelech, their brother, who murdered them, and upon the leaders of Shechem, who strengthened his hands to murder his brothers.”

notes.570: (tn, Heb): “set against him bandits.” Putting bandits in the hills. This piracy certainly interrupted or discouraged trade, and probably deprived Abimelech of tariffs or tribute. See C. F. Burney, Judges, 277; G. F. Moore, Judges (ICC), 253.

notes.573: (sn): The name Gaal derives from, or at least sounds like, a Hebrew verb meaning “to abhor, loathe.” His father’s name, Ebed, means “servant.” Perhaps then this could be translated, “loathsome one, son of a servant.” This individual’s very name (which may be the narrator’s nickname for him, not his actual name) seems to hint at his immoral character and lowly social status.
notes.574: (tn, Heb): “trusted in him.” Here the verb probably describes more than a mental attitude. It is likely that the Shechemites made an alliance with Gaal and were now trusting him for protection in return for their loyalty (and probably tribute).

rashi.heb:
*געל בן עבד.* 
מאומה אחרת היה:
rashi.eng: *Gaal the son of Ebed.* He was from another nation.

notes.576: (tn, Heb): “stomped” or “trampled.” This refers to the way in which the juice was squeezed out in the wine vats by stepping on the grapes with one’s bare feet. For a discussion of grape harvesting in ancient Israel, see O. Borowski, Agriculture in Iron Age Israel, 110-14.

rashi.heb:
*ויעשו הלולים.* 
(תרגום:) ועבדו חנגין:
rashi.eng: *וַיַּעֲשוּ הִלּולִים.* And they made dances [quoting Targum Jonathan].

notes.579: (tn, Heb): “him”; the referent (Abimelech) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

rashi.heb:
*מי אבימלך ומי שכם.* 
מי אבימלך להיות שר על שכם ומי שכם להיות עבדים לאבימלך, הלא בן ירובעל היה אבימלך מן עפרת אבי העזרי (לעיל ו יא):
rashi.eng: *Who is Abimelech and who is Shechem.* Who is Abimelech that he should rule over Shechem, and who is Shechem to be servants to Abimelech? Was not Abimelech the son of Jerubbaal (הֲלֹא בֶן יַרֻבַּעַל) from Ophrah of the Abiezrites?

rashi.heb:
*וזבל פקידו.* 
וזה פקיד העיר ששמו 'זבול', פקידו של אבימלך הוא, ואדוניו אין לו משפט מלוכה בעיר ואף פקידו אינו כלום:
rashi.eng: *and Zebul (is he not) his officer.* As for the officer of the city whose name is Zebul, he is (but) an officer of Abimelech; since his master has no right to rule here, neither do his appointees.

rashi.heb:
*עבדו את אנשי חמור.* 
אם באתם לקנות לכם אדונים, באו ועבדו את אנשי חמור, שהיה נשיא הארץ מקדם (בראשית לד ב):
rashi.eng: *Serve the men of Hamor.* If you are coming to acquire for yourselves leaders, come and serve the men of Hamor, who was a previous lord over the land.

rashi.heb:
*ומדוע נעבדנו.* 
לאבימלך:
rashi.eng: *but why should we serve him.* I.e., Abimelech.

notes.581: (tn, Heb): “in my hand.” If only these men were under my command. One might assume from v. 26b that the men were already at his disposal, but perhaps that was not one of the terms of the agreement. Another possibility is that v. 26 is a general summary statement, with vv. 27-29 then detailing how the alliance with Gaal came about.
notes.582: (tn, Heb): “said to Abimelech.” On the other hand, the preposition ל (lamed) prefixed to the proper name may be vocative (see R. G. Boling, Judges [AB], 178). If so, one could translate, “He boasted, ‘Abimelech…’”

rashi.heb:
*ויאמר לאבימלך.* 
ויאמר געל בפני זבול, הודיע לאבימלך:
rashi.eng: *And he said to Abimelech.* (Indirectly;) and Gaal spoke before Zebul to inform Abimelech (as subsequently evident).

rashi.heb:
*רבה צבאך וצאה.* 
מן המקום שאתה שם, ונראה את גדולתך:
rashi.eng: *Increase your army, and come out.* From the place where you are, and let us see your greatness.

notes.586: (tn): The form בְּתָרְמָה (b�tarmah) in the Hebrew text, which occurs only here, has traditionally been understood to mean “secretly” or “with deception.” If this is correct, it is derived from II רָמָה (ramah, “to deceive”). Some interpreters object, pointing out that this would imply Zebul was trying to deceive Abimelech, which is clearly not the case in this context. But this objection is unwarranted. If retained, the phrase would refer instead to deceptive measures used by Zebul to avoid the suspicion of Gaal when he dispatched the messengers from Shechem. The present translation assumes an emendation to “in Arumah” (בָּארוּמָה, ba’rumah), a site mentioned in v. 41 as the headquarters of Abimelech. Confusion of alef and tav in archaic Hebrew script, while uncommon, is certainly not unimaginable.
notes.588: (tn): The participle, as used here, suggests Gaal and his brothers are in the process of arriving, but the preceding verses imply they have already settled in. Perhaps Zebul uses understatement to avoid the appearance of negligence on his part. After all, if he made the situation sound too bad, Abimelech, when he was informed, might ask why he had allowed this rebellion to reach such a stage.
notes.589: (tn): The words “to rebel” are interpretive. The precise meaning of the Hebrew verb צוּר (tsur) is unclear here. It is best to take it in the sense of “to instigate; to incite; to provoke” (see Deut 2:9, 19 and R. G. Boling, Judges [AB], 178).

rashi.heb:
*בתרמה.* 
כמו במרמה, בתרמית, כלומר: בלט ובסתר:
rashi.eng: *in secret.* Heb. בְּתָרְמָה. As in (Gen. 27:35) “בְּמִרְמָה,” and (Jer. 8: 5) “בּתַרְמִית,” i.e., quietly and secretly.

notes.591: (tn, Heb): “you and the people who are with you.”
notes.592: (tn): The words “outside the city” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

notes.593: (tn, Heb): “Look! He and the people who are with him will come out to you, and you will do to him what your hand finds [to do].”

notes.594: (tn, Heb): “and all the people who were with him arose.”
notes.595: (tn, Heb): “four heads.” The words “they divided into” are supplied in the translation for clarification.

rashi.heb:
*ארבע ראשים.* 
ארבעה כתות:
rashi.eng: *in four companies.* Lit. in four heads.

notes.596: (tn, Heb): “the people” (also in vv. 38, 43, 48). These were warriors, so “men” has been used in the translation, since in ancient Israelite culture soldiers would have been exclusively males.
notes.597: (tn, Heb): “the shadow on the hills you are seeing, like men.”

notes.598: (tn, Heb): “navel.” On the background of the Hebrew expression “the navel of the land,” see R. G. Boling, Judges (AB), 178-79.
notes.600: (tn, Heb): Some English translations simply transliterated this as a place name ( “Elon-meonenim”); cf. NAB, NRSV.

rashi.heb:
*מעם טבור הארץ.* 
(תרגום:) מן תוקפא דארעא, מהר הגבוה שבכולם:
rashi.eng: *from the navel of the earth.* (Targum Jonathan renders) מִן תּוּקְפָא דְאַרְעָא (i. e., from the strength of the land) from its highest mountain. Combine 2 Heb. words

rashi.heb:
*אלון מעוננים.* 
(תרגום:) מישר מעוננים:
rashi.eng: *plain Meonenim.* the plain of Meonenim.

notes.604: (tn, Heb): “So Gaal went out before the leaders of Shechem.”

notes.605: (tn, Heb): “he”; the referent (Gaal) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
notes.606: (tn): The word “Shechemites” is not in the Hebrew text, but is supplied for clarification.

notes.607: (tc, Heb): “stayed.” Some scholars revise the vowel pointing on this verb from that of the MT, resulting in the translation “and he returned to.” The Lucianic recension of the LXX understands the word in this way.

notes.609: (tn, Heb): “the people”; the referent (the Shechemites) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

rashi.heb:
*ויצא העם השדה.* 
אנשי שכם:
rashi.eng: *that the people went out to the field.* The people of Shechem.

rashi.heb:
*ויגידו.* 
המגידים לאבימלך, שיצאו בני העיר אל השדה לעשות חפציהם:
rashi.eng: *and they told.* The informers told Abimelech that the citizens went out to the field to attend their needs.

notes.612: (tn, Heb): “And he saw and, look, the people were coming out of the city.”
notes.613: (tn, Heb): “he arose against them and struck them.”

notes.614: (tn): Or possibly, “the unit that was with him.”

rashi.heb:
*פתח שער העיר.* 
שלא יוכלו ליכנס:
rashi.eng: *in the entrance of the gate of the city.* So that no one could enter.

notes.617: (tn, Heb): “sowed it with salt.” The spreading of salt over the city was probably a symbolic act designed to place the site under a curse, deprive it of fertility, and prevent any future habitation. The practice is referred to outside the Bible as well. For example, one of the curses in the Aramaic Sefire treaty states concerning Arpad: “May Hadad sow in them salt and weeds, and may it not be mentioned again!” See J. A. Fitzmyer, The Aramaic Inscriptions of Sefire (BibOr), 15, 53. Deut 29:23, Jer 17:6, and Zeph 2:9 associate salt flats or salty regions with infertility and divine judgment.

notes.618: (sn): Perhaps the Tower of Shechem was a nearby town, distinct from Shechem proper, or a tower within the city.
notes.619: (tn): Apparently this rare word refers here to the most inaccessible area of the temple, perhaps the inner sanctuary or an underground chamber. It appears only here and in 1 Sam 13:6, where it is paired with “cisterns” and refers to subterranean or cave-like hiding places.
notes.620: (sn): The name El-Berith means “God of the Covenant.” It is probably a reference to the Canaanite high god El.

rashi.heb:
*צריח.* 
יער שכפו אילנות ופסגים סביב סביב, וקורין אותו פלייש"ר בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *forest.* צְרִיחַ in Heb. A forest in which the trees and branches are bent over all around the forest; plissé in O. F.

rashi.heb:
*בית אל ברית.* 
אותו צריח היה של בעל ברית, שם של עבודה זרה שלהם, וצלמון (פסוק מח), יער היה שם ויש פותרין: צריח, וודוו"י בלע"ז שעושין בקרקע:
rashi.eng: *Beth-El-Brith.* That forest belonged to Baal Brith (above v. 4), the name of their idol. Zalmon (v. 48) also had a forest. Some interpret צְרִיחַ as voutes in O.F., which is made in the ground.

notes.621: (tn, Heb): “and it was told to Abimelech.”

notes.624: (tn, Heb): “Abimelech.” The proper name has been replaced with the pronoun (“he”) due to considerations of English style.
notes.625: (tn): The Hebrew text has the plural here.
notes.627: (tn, Heb): “What you have seen me do, quickly do like me.”

rashi.heb:
*שוכת עצים.* 
ענף עצים:
rashi.eng: *שוֹכַת עֵצִים.* A bough from a tree.

notes.628: (tn): The words “the branches” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
notes.629: (tn, Heb): “they kindled over them the stronghold with fire.”
notes.630: (tn): Or “men,” but the word seems to have a more general sense here, as the conclusion to the sentence suggests.

notes.632: (tn, Heb): “he camped near Thebez and captured it.”

notes.634: (tn): Or “fortress.” The same Hebrew term occurs once more in this verse and twice in v. 52.

notes.635: (sn): A hand mill consisted of an upper stone and larger lower stone. One would turn the upper stone with a handle to grind the grain, which was placed between the stones. An upper millstone, which was typically about two inches thick and a foot or so in diameter, probably weighed 25-30 pounds (11.4-13.6 kg). See G. F. Moore, Judges (ICC), 268; C. F. Burney, Judges, 288.
notes.636: (tn, Heb): “Abimelech’s.” The proper name has been replaced by the pronoun “his” in the translation in keeping with conventions of English narrative style.

rashi.heb:
*פלח רכב.* 
חתיכת אבן של ריחים העליונה הקרויה רכב:
rashi.eng: *פֶּלַח רֶכֶב.* A piece of the upper millstone which is called a רֶכֶב.

rashi.heb:
*ותרץ.* 
ותרוצץ:
rashi.eng: *and crushed.* וְתָרִץ same as וּתְרוֹצֵץ (a more familiar form).

notes.637: (tn): The Hebrew text adds, “and said to him.” This has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.
notes.638: (tn): The Hebrew text adds, “concerning me.” This has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.

rashi.heb:
*פן יאמרו לי.* 
פן יאמרו עלי:
rashi.eng: *lest they say of me.* Lit. lest they say to me.

notes.642: (tn): The word “death” has been supplied in the translation for clarification.

rashi.heb:
*בן דודו.* 
כך שמו:
rashi.eng: *the sons of Dodo.* Heb. דוֹדוֹ, this was his name.

notes.646: (sn): The name Habboth Jair means “tent villages of Jair” in Hebrew.
notes.647: (tn, Heb): “they call them Havvoth Jair to this day – which are in the land of Gilead.”

rashi.heb:
*עירים.* 
(תרגום:) עולין, סוסים בחורים:
rashi.eng: *עֲיָרִים.* (Targum Jonathan renders) עוּלִין, i.e., colts.

rashi.heb:
*ושלשים עירים להם.* 
ושלשים ערים בלא חומה להם, לכך נקראו עירים, לשון עיירות:
rashi.eng: *And they had thirty cities.* And they had thirty unwalled cities. It therefore states עֲיָרִים which is an expression of unwalled cities (עֲיָירוֹת).

notes.648: (tn, Heb): “in the eyes of the Lord.”
notes.650: (sn): The Ashtars were local manifestations of the goddess Ashtar (i.e., Astarte).
notes.651: (map): For location see Map1-A1; JP3-F3; JP4-F3.
notes.652: (tn, Heb): “the gods of Syria, the gods of Sidon, the gods of Moab, the gods of the Ammonites, and the gods of the Philistines.”

rashi.heb:
*את הבעלים וגו'.* 
שבע עבודות זרות נמנו כאן:
rashi.eng: *the Baalim, etc..* Seven idols are enumerated here.

rashi.heb:
*ויעזבו את ה' ולא עבדוהו.* 
אפילו בשותפות עם אלו:
rashi.eng: *and they forsook the Lord, and did not serve Him.* Even in conjunction with the idols.

notes.654: (tn): Or “the Lord’s anger burned [or “raged”] against Israel.”
notes.655: (tn, Heb): “sold them into the hands of.”

notes.656: (tn, Heb): “shattered and crushed.” The repetition of similar sounding synonyms (רָעַץ [ra’ats] and רָצַץ [ratsats]) is for emphasis; רָצַץ appears in the Polel, adding further emphasis to the affirmation.
notes.657: (tn): The phrase שְׁמֹנֶה עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה (shemoneh ’esreh shanah) could be translated “eighteen years,” but this would be difficult after the reference to “that year.” It is possible that v. 8b is parenthetical, referring to an eighteen year long period of oppression east of the Jordan which culminated in hostilities against all Israel (including Judah, see v. 9) in the eighteenth year. It is simpler to translate the phrase as an ordinal number, though the context does not provide the point of reference. (See Gen 14:4-5 and R. G. Boling, Judges [AB], 191-92.) In this case, the following statement specifies which “Israelites” are in view.

rashi.heb:
*בשנה ההיא.* 
כשמת יאיר:
rashi.eng: *that year.* When Jair died.

rashi.heb:
*אשר בעבר הירדן.* 
ארץ ראובן וגד וחצי המנשה, שהיו שכניהם:
rashi.eng: *(the children of Israel) that were beyond the Jordan.* I.e., The land of Reuben, Gad, and half of Menasseh who were their neighbors.

notes.659: (tn): Or “Israel experienced great distress.” Perhaps here the verb has the nuance “hemmed in.”

rashi.heb:
*הלא ממצרים.* 
שבע תשועות יש כאן, כנגד שבע עבודות זרות שהיו עובדים:
rashi.eng: *Did (I) not (save you) from the Egyptians.* Seven deliverances are mentioned here, corresponding to the seven heathen gods that they served.

notes.661: (tc): The translation follows the LXX which reads “Midian”; the Hebrew text has “Maon.”
notes.662: (tn): The words “Did I not deliver you” are interpretive. The Hebrew text simply reads, “Is it not from Egypt…when they oppressed you?” Perhaps the incomplete sentence reflects the Lord’s frustration.

rashi.heb:
*ומעון.* 
שם אומה:
rashi.eng: *and Maon.* This is the name of a nation.

notes.666: (tn, Heb): “according to all whatever is good in your eyes.”
notes.667: (sn): You do to us as you see fit, but deliver us today. The request seems contradictory, but it can be explained in one of two ways. They may be asking for relief from their enemies and direct discipline from God’s hand. Or they may mean, “In the future you can do whatever you like to us, but give us relief from what we’re suffering right now.”

notes.670: (tn, Heb): “And his spirit grew short [i.e., impatient] with the suffering of Israel.” The Hebrew noun נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh) also appears as the subject of the verb קָצַר (qatsar) in Num 21:4 (the Israelites grow impatient wandering in the wilderness), Judg 16:16 (Samson grows impatient with Delilah’s constant nagging), and Zech 11:8 (Zechariah grows impatient with the three negligent “shepherds”).

rashi.heb:
*ותקצר נפשו בעמל.* 
כביכול לא היה רחבת מקום לסבול ולכנס שם צרה שהיה לו בעמל ישראל:
rashi.eng: *and His soul was grieved by the toil.* As if one could say, He did not have the expanse to endure and contain the anguish caused Him by the toil (or suffering) Of Israel.

rashi.heb:
*ויצעקו.* 
נאספו על ידי כרוז:
rashi.eng: *were gathered.* Heb. וַיִּצְּעֲקוּ. They gathered through announcements.

notes.673: (tn, Heb): “Who is the man who will begin fighting.”

notes.674: (tn, Heb): “Now he was the son of a woman, a prostitute, and Gilead fathered Jephthah.”

notes.676: (tn, Heb): “in the house of our father.”

notes.679: (tn, Heb): “Empty men joined themselves to Jephthah and went out with him.”

rashi.heb:
*וילחמו בני עמון.* 
היא האמורה למעלה (י ט):
rashi.eng: *and the children of Ammon made war.* (The war) referred to above.

notes.680: (tn, Heb): “When the Ammonites fought with Israel.”

notes.684: (tn, Heb): “Did you not hate me and make me leave?”

notes.685: (tn, Heb): “therefore”; “even so.” For MT לָכֵן (lakhen, “therefore”) the LXX has an opposite reading, “not so,” which seems to be based on the Hebrew words לֹא כֵן (lo’ khen).
notes.686: (tn, Heb): “we have returned to you.” For another example of שׁוּב אֶל (shuv ’el) in the sense of “give allegiance to,” see 1 Kgs 12:27b.
notes.687: (sn): Then you will become the leader. The leaders of Gilead now use the word רֹאשׁ (ro’sh, “head, leader”), the same term that appeared in their original, general offer (see 10:18). In their initial offer to Jephthah they had simply invited him to be their קָצִין (qatsin, “commander”; v. 6). When he resists they must offer him a more attractive reward – rulership over the region. See R. G. Boling, Judges (AB), 198.
notes.688: (tn, Heb): “leader of us and all who live in Gilead.”

notes.689: (tn): “All right” is supplied in the translation for clarification.
notes.691: (tn): Some translate the final statement as a question, “will I really be your leader?” An affirmative sentence is preferable. Jephthah is repeating the terms of the agreement in an official manner. In v. 10 the leaders legally agree to these terms.

notes.692: (tn, Heb): “The Lord will be the one who hears between us.” For the idiom שָׁמַע בַּיִן (shama’ bayin, “to hear between”), see Deut 1:16.
notes.693: (sn): The Lord will judge…if we do not do as you say. The statement by the leaders of Gilead takes the form of a legally binding oath, which obligates them to the terms of the agreement.

notes.694: (tn, Heb): “spoke all his words.” This probably refers to the “words” recorded in v. 9. Jephthah repeats the terms of the agreement at the Lord’s sanctuary, perhaps to ratify the contract or to emphasize the Gileadites’ obligation to keep their part of the bargain. Another option is to translate, “Jephthah conducted business before the Lord in Mizpah.” In this case, the statement is a general reference to the way Jephthah ruled. He recognized the Lord’s authority and made his decisions before the Lord.

rashi.heb:
*את כל דבריו.* 
התנאי שביניהם:
rashi.eng: *all his words.* The stipulation which was between them.

rashi.heb:
*לפני ה' במצפה.* 
למקום שנאספו כולם, שהשכינה שורה על רוב צבור:
rashi.eng: *before the Lord in Mizpah.* At the place where they all gathered (above 10:17), since the Divine Presence resides amongst the multitudes of the congregation.

notes.695: (tn, Heb): “What to me and to you that…?”

notes.698: (tn, Heb): “from the Arnon to the Jabbok and to the Jordan.” The word “River” has been supplied in the translation with “Arnon” and “Jabbok,” because these are less familiar to modern readers than the Jordan.
notes.699: (tc): The translation assumes a singular suffix (“[return] it”); the Hebrew text has a plural suffix (“[return] them”), which, if retained, might refer to the cities of the land.

notes.701: (tn, Heb): “For when they went up from.”

rashi.heb:
*עד ים סוף.* 
בדרומה של ארץ אדום, וארץ אדום בדרומה של ארץ כנען:
rashi.eng: *up to the Red Sea.* Located south of the land of Edom which is itself located to the south of the land of Canaan.

notes.705: (tn, Heb): “Also to the king of Moab he sent, but he was unwilling.”

rashi.heb:
*אעברה נא בארצך.* 
מדרום לצפון, ליכנס לארץ כנען:
rashi.eng: *Let me pass now through your land.* From the South to the North to enter the land of Canaan.

rashi.heb:
*וגם אל מלך מואב.* 
שהיתה ארצו בסוף ארץ אדום, במזרחה של אדום ובדרומה של ארץ ישראל:
rashi.eng: *and also to the king of Moab.* Whose land was adjacent to the land of Edom along the east, and was to the south of the land of Israel.

rashi.heb:
*ולא אבה.* 
משה רמזה בתורה (דברים ב כט): כאשר עשו לי בני עשו היושבים בשעיר והמואבים היושבים בער, כשם שאדום לא נתנום לעבור, כך מואב לא נתנום לעבור:
rashi.eng: *and he was unwilling.* Moses hinted this in the Torah (Deut. 2: 29), “As was done to me by the children of Esau who dwell in Seir (Edom) and by the Moabites who dwell in Ar,” implying that just as Edom did not let them pass, similarly Moab did not let them pass.

notes.706: (tn, Heb): “he”; the referent (Israel; the pronoun in the Hebrew text represents a collective singular) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
notes.707: (tn): The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but has been supplied in the translation for clarity.

rashi.heb:
*וילך במדבר.* 
מן המערב למזרח, במיצר דרומי של אדום ומואב:
rashi.eng: *And they went through the wilderness.* From west to east along the southern border of Edom and Moab.

rashi.heb:
*ויסב את ארץ אדום.* 
כל דרומה:
rashi.eng: *and went around the land of Edom.* Its entire southern border.

rashi.heb:
*ואת ארץ מואב.* 
כל דרומה, וכשהגיע למקצוע דרומית מזרחית, פנה אל הצפון לסבוב את מיצר המזרחי:
rashi.eng: *and the land of Moab.* The entire southern border, and when they reached the southeastern corner they turned north to compass the eastern border.

rashi.heb:
*ויבא ממזרח שמש לארץ מואב ויחנון בעבר ארנון.* 
לסוף מזרחה של ארץ מואב, ושם התחילה ארץ סיחון ועוג, וכבשו עבר הירדן במזרח ארץ כנען ועברו הירדן, ונכנסו לה לארץ כנען דרך המזרח:
rashi.eng: *and they came to the east of the land of Moab, and they encamped on the other side of the Arnon.* To the end of the eastern border of the land of Moab whence began the land of Sichon and Og. They then conquered the side of the Jordan to the east of the land of Canaan (as the following verses indicate), and then crossed the Jordan, entering the land of Canaan from the east.

notes.709: (tn, Heb): “Sihon.” The proper name (“Sihon”) has been replaced in the translation by the pronoun (“he”) because of English style; a repetition of the proper name here would be redundant in English.
notes.710: (tn, Heb): “all his people” (also in the following verse).

notes.711: (tn): That is, took as its own possession.

notes.712: (tn, Heb): “from the Arnon to the Jabbok, and from the desert to the Jordan.” The word “River” has been supplied in the translation with “Arnon” and “Jabbok,” because these are less familiar to modern readers than the Jordan.

rashi.heb:
*ויירשו וגו' מארנון ועד היבק.* 
שאתה אומר שהוא שלך (פסוק יג), הם מסיחון לקחו:
rashi.eng: *And they possessed… from the Arnon up to the Jabbok.* That which you say was yours, (in reality) they (i.e., our forefathers) took it from Sichon.

rashi.heb:
*ומן המדבר ועד הירדן.* 
מדברות היו שם לפני הירדן:
rashi.eng: *and from the wilderness up to the Jordan.* There were deserts situated east of the Jordan.

notes.715: (tn, Heb): “will you dispossess him [i.e., Israel; or possibly “it,” i.e., the territory]?” There is no interrogative marker in the Hebrew text.

notes.716: (tn, Heb): “Is it not so that what Chemosh your god causes you to possess, you possess, and all whom the Lord our God dispossesses before us we will possess?” Jephthah speaks of Chemosh as if he is on a par with the Lord God of Israel. This does not necessarily mean that Jephthah is polytheistic or that he recognizes the Lord as only a local deity. He may simply be assuming the Ammonite king’s perspective for the sake of argument. Other texts, as well as the extrabiblical Mesha inscription, associate Chemosh with Moab, while Milcom is identified as the god of the Ammonites. Why then does Jephthah refer to Chemosh as the Ammonite god? Ammon had likely conquered Moab and the Ammonite king probably regarded himself as heir of all territory formerly held by Moab. Originally Moab had owned the disputed territory (cf. Num 21:26-29), meaning that Chemosh was regarded as the god of the region (see R. G. Boling, Judges [AB], 203-4). Jephthah argues that Chemosh had long ago relinquished claim to the area (by allowing Sihon to conquer it), while the Lord had long ago established jurisdiction over it (by taking it from Sihon and giving it to Israel). Both sides should abide by the decisions of the gods which had stood firm for three hundred years.

notes.717: (tn): The Hebrew grammatical constructions of all three rhetorical questions indicate emphasis, which “really” and “dare to” are intended to express in the translation. Jephthah argues that the Ammonite king should follow the example of Balak, who, once thwarted in his attempt to bring a curse on Israel, refused to attack Israel and returned home (Num 22-24).

rashi.heb:
*על ידי ארנון.* 
אצל ארנון, שהיו ממואב, וידעו שלא היה להם לעבור עליהם, שהרי מסיחון כבשום (במדבר כא כד), שלקחם ממלך מואב (שם שם כו):
rashi.eng: *עַל יְדֵי אַרְנוֹן.* (Lit., on the hands of Arnon) I.e., along Arnon. These cities were from Moab, but they realized that they could not instigate war over them because Israel had conquered them from Sichon who had taken them from the king of Moab.

rashi.heb:
*שלש מאות שנה.* 
משכבשו את הארץ בימי יהושע עד יפתח מכאן יש ללמוד שנות השופטים הנזכרים עד הנה, אם שני השעבוד של כל אומה נמנים בתוך ימי השופט אם לאו. שנינו בסדר עולם (פרק יב): יהושע פרנס את ישראל עשרים ושמונה שנה, ואין לו מקרא ממי ללמוד. עתניאל (לעיל ג יא), ארבעים שנה, ושני שעבוד של כושן רשעתים (שם שם ח), בכללם אחריו אהוד (שם שם ל), שמונים שנה, שמונה עשרה שנים, שעבוד של עגלון (שם שם יד) בתוכם, הרי מאה ארבעים ושמונה שנה. דבורה (שם ה לא) ארבעים שנה, ושני שעבוד יבין (שם ד ג) בתוכם, הרי מאה שמונים ושמונה. אחריו, שבע שנים של שעבוד מדין (שם ו א), וארבעים של גדעון (שם ח כח), ושלש של אבימלך (שם ט כב), הרי מאתים שלשים ושמונה שנים. אחריו, עשרים ושלש של תולע (שם י ב), ועשרים ושתים של יאיר (שם י ג), אלא שעלתה שנה אחת לשניהם, ושמונה עשרה של בני עמון (שם שם ח) עד שלא בא יפתח, הרי שלש מאות:
rashi.eng: *three hundred years.* Since the land was conquered in the days of Joshua until Jephthah. From here we can derive if the periods of the judges that were mentioned up to this point include the years of oppression by the heathens or not. We have learned in Seder Olam (Ch. 12): Joshua led Israel twenty eight years, but I have no Scripture whence to derive it. Othniel led them forty years including the years of oppression by Cushan-rishathaim (above 3:11); after him was Ehud for eighty years (above 3:30) including the eighteen years of oppression by Eglon. This totals one hundred forty eight years. Deborah led them forty years (above 5:31) including the years of oppression by Jabin. This totals one hundred eighty eight years; afterwards were the seven years of oppression by Midian (above 6:1) and the forty years of Gideon (above 8: 28), then the three of Abimelech (above 9:22), thus totaling two hundred thirty eight years. Afterwards were the twenty three of Tola, and the twenty two of Jair (above 10:2,3), however one same year coincides for both of them; finally, adding the eighteen of Ammon prior to Jephthah’s introduction (above 10:8), this amounts to the three hundred years.

notes.721: (tn, Heb): “Jephthah’s words which he sent to him.”

notes.724: (tn, Heb): “From Mizpah in Gilead he passed through [to] the Ammonites.”

rashi.heb:
*עבר בני עמון.* 
אל בני עמון:
rashi.eng: *עָבַר בְּנֵי עַמּוֹן.* (Lit., he passed the children of Ammon) I.e., he passed over to the children of Ammon.

notes.725: (tn, Heb): “the one coming out, who comes out from.” The text uses a masculine singular participle with prefixed article, followed by a relative pronoun and third masculine singular verb. The substantival masculine singular participle הַיּוֹצֵא (hayyotse’, “the one coming out”) is used elsewhere of inanimate objects (such as a desert [Num 21:13] or a word [Num 32:24]) or persons (Jer 5:6; 21:9; 38:2). In each case context must determine the referent. Jephthah may have envisioned an animal meeting him, since the construction of Iron Age houses would allow for an animal coming through the doors of a house (see R. G. Boling, Judges [AB], 208). But the fact that he actually does offer up his daughter indicates the language of the vow is fluid enough to encompass human beings, including women. He probably intended such an offering from the very beginning, but he obviously did not expect his daughter to meet him first.
notes.726: (tn): The language is fluid enough to include women and perhaps even animals, but the translation uses the masculine pronoun because the Hebrew form is grammatically masculine.
notes.727: (tn): Some translate “or,” suggesting that Jephthah makes a distinction between humans and animals. According to this view, if a human comes through the door, then Jephthah will commit him/her to the Lord’s service, but if an animal comes through the doors, he will offer it up as a sacrifice. However, it is far more likely that the Hebrew construction (vav [ו] + perfect) specifies how the subject will become the Lord’s, that is, by being offered up as a sacrifice. For similar constructions, where the apodosis of a conditional sentence has at least two perfects (each with vav) in sequence, see Gen 34:15-16; Exod 18:16.

notes.730: (tn, Heb): “The Ammonites were humbled before the Israelites.”

rashi.heb:
*אבל כרמים.* 
(תרגום:) מישר כרמיא:
rashi.eng: *Abel Cheramim.* The plain of vineyards [after Targum Jonathan].

notes.731: (tn, Heb): “Look! His daughter was coming out.”

notes.733: (tn, Heb): “you have brought me very low,” or “you have knocked me to my knees.” The infinitive absolute precedes the verb for emphasis.
notes.734: (tn, Heb): “You are among [or “like”] those who trouble me.”
notes.735: (tn, Heb): “I opened my mouth to the Lord and I am not able to return.”

rashi.heb:
*הכרע הכרעתני.* 
לשון נקבה, ודומה לו (שיר השירים ד ט): לבבתני אחותי כלה:
rashi.eng: *הַכְרֵע ַהִכְרַעְתִּנִי.* This is expressed in feminine form (the “tav” being vocalized with a חִירִיק) as in, (Song of Songs 4:9) לִבַּבְתִּנִי אֲחֹתִי כַלָּה (“You drew my heart, my sister, my beloved”).

rashi.heb:
*היית בעוכרי.* 
כל דמי נעכר, קפחת את רגלי:
rashi.eng: *(you) have become one of those that trouble me.* All my blood is troubled. You have ruined my equilibrium (lit., feet thus causing me to fall).

notes.736: (tn): The conjunction “since” is supplied in the translation for clarification.
notes.737: (tn, Heb): “you opened your mouth to the Lord, do to me according to [what] went out from your mouth.”

notes.739: (tn, Heb): “Let this thing be done for me.”
notes.740: (tn, Heb): “Leave me alone for two months so I can go and go down on the hills and weep over my virginity – I and my friends.”

rashi.heb:
*וירדתי על ההרים.* 
לשון יללה הוא, ודוגמתו (ישעיהו טו ג): על גגותיה וברחובותיה כולה ייליל ירד בבכי, המתעצב בבכי עד שגופו משתבר ובמדרש אגדה דורש רבי תנחומא (בחוקותי ה): על ההרים. לפני סנהדרין, שמא ימצאו פתח לנדרך:
.
rashi.eng: *and wail upon the mountains.* This is an expression of lamenting, as in (Isa. 15:3) “Upon her roofs and streets they all lament, lamenting with a cry יוֹרֵד בַּבֶּכִי)),” as one who is immersed in mourning until his body is broken (since יְרִידָה is also an expression of “breaking,” as in Lamen. 1:13)In an Aggadic interpretation Rabbi Tanchuma (Behukosai) explains “Upon the mountains” as referring to (her) presenting the case before the Sanhedrin (Great Court); perhaps they can find an opening to your (i.e., Jephthah’s) vow.

notes.742: (tn, Heb): “on the hills.” The words “as she walked” are supplied.

rashi.heb:
*ותבך על בתוליה.* 
מדלא כתיב על בתולותיה, משמע בתולים ממש:
rashi.eng: *and she cried over her virginity.* Heb. בְּתוּלֶיהָ. Since it does not say “over her maidens” (בְּתוּלוֹתֶיהָ), it implies that this refers to her actual virginity.

notes.743: (tn, Heb): “She had never known a man.” Some understand this to mean that her father committed her to a life of celibacy, but the disjunctive clause (note the vav + subject + verb pattern) more likely describes her condition at the time the vow was fulfilled. (See G. F. Moore, Judges [ICC], 302-3; C. F. Burney, Judges, 324.) She died a virgin and never experienced the joys of marriage and motherhood.
notes.744: (tn, Heb): “There was a custom in Israel.”

rashi.heb:
*ותהי חק.* 
גזרו שלא יעשה אדם עוד כן, שאלו הלך אצל פנחס, או הוא בא אצלו, היה מתיר לו נדרו, עמדו בגדולתן, ומבין שניהם אבדה, ונפרע מהם, פנחס נסתלקה שכינה הימנו, שנאמר בדברי הימים (א ט כ): לפנים ה' עמו, למדנו שבסופו אינו עמו, ויפתח הוכה בשחין וניפול אברים, שנאמר (לקמן יב ז): ויקבר בערי גלעד. ויש עוד לפתור: ותהי חק בישראל. מחובר למקרא שלאחריו:
rashi.eng: *and it was a statute.* They decreed that no one should do this anymore (i.e., they publicized that no one should offer a human being), because had Jephthah gone to Phinehas or vice versa, he would have nullified his (i.e., Jephthah’s) vow (i.e., he would have instructed him what the law is in such an instance). However, they were particular about their honor, and as a result she was destroyed. Consequently, they were punished; Phinehas, by the Divine presence leaving him as it is stated in (I) Chron. (9:20) “Previously God was with him,” so we see subsequently God was not with him; and Jephthah was afflicted with boils and dismemberment as it is stated, (below 12:7) “And he was buried in the cities [pl.] of Gilead.” (His limbs were buried in the various cities.) We can also interpret “And it was a statute in Israel” as connected to the following verse.

notes.745: (tn, Heb): “From days to days,” a Hebrew idiom for “annually.”
notes.746: (tn, Heb): “go to commemorate.” The rare Hebrew verb תָּנָה (tanah, “to tell; to repeat; to recount”) occurs only here and in 5:11.
notes.747: (tn): The Hebrew text adds, “in the year.” This is redundant (note “every year” at the beginning of the verse) and has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.

rashi.heb:
*מימים ימימה תלכנה וגו'.* 
הדבר הזה קבעו עליהם לחוק:
rashi.eng: *from year to year….* This they (i.e., the daughters of Israel) accepted upon themselves as a statute.

rashi.heb:
*לתנות.* 
לקונן:
rashi.eng: *lament.*  To lament.

notes.748: (tn, Heb): “the men of Ephraim were summoned [or “were mustered”].”
notes.751: (tn, Heb): “Your house we will burn over you with fire.”

rashi.heb:
*ויעבור צפונה.* 
ויעבור את הירדן, והלכו לצפון עבר הירדן, אל הגלעד:
rashi.eng: *and passed to the north.* They crossed the Jordan (eastward) and went up north to Gilead.

notes.752: (tn, Heb): A man of great strife I was and my people and the Ammonites.”

notes.754: (tn, Heb): “you were no deliverer.” Codex Alexandrinus (A) of the LXX has “no one was helping.”
notes.755: (tn, Heb): “I put my life in my hand.”
notes.757: (tn): The Hebrew adds “against me” here. This is redundant in English and has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.

notes.759: (tc, Heb): “Refugees of Ephraim are you, O Gilead, in the midst of Ephraim and in the midst of Manasseh.” The LXX omits the entire second half of the verse (beginning with “because”). The words כִּי אָמְרוּ פְּלִיטֵי אֶפְרַיִם (ki ’amru p�litey ’efrayim, “because they said, ‘Refugees of Ephraim’”) may have been accidentally copied from the next verse (cf. כִּי יֹאמְרוּ פְּלִיטֵי אֶפְרַיִם, ki yo’m�ru pelitey ’efrayim) and the following words (“you, O Gilead…Manasseh”) then added in an attempt to make sense of the verse. See G. F. Moore, Judges (ICC), 307-8, and C. F. Burney, Judges, 327. If the Hebrew text is retained, then the Ephraimites appear to be insulting the Gileadites by describing them as refugees who are squatting on Ephraim’s and Manasseh’s land. The present translation assumes that “Ephraim” is a genitive of location after “refugees.”

rashi.heb:
*כי אמרו פליטי אפרים אתם גלעד.* 
פחותים שבאפרים היו מבזים את הגלעד, ואומרים להם: מה אתם גלעד חשובים בתוך אפרים ובתוך מנשה, כן תרגם יונתן:
rashi.eng: *because the lowest of Ephraim said, (Of what importance are) you Gileadites.* The lowly of Ephraim belittled Gilead by saying to them, “Of what importance are you Gilead among Ephraim and Menasseh.” So renders Targum Jonathan.

notes.760: (tn): The word “River” is not in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for clarification.
notes.761: (tn): Or “against Ephraim,” that is, so as to prevent Ephraim from crossing.
notes.762: (tn): The Hebrew text has a plural form here.

rashi.heb:
*וילכוד גלעד את מעברות וגו'.* 
היו שומרים במקום המעברות:
rashi.eng: *And the Gileadites seized the fords….* They established guards at the fords.

notes.764: (sn): The inability of the Ephraimites to pronounce the word shibboleth the way the Gileadites did served as an identifying test. It illustrates that during this period there were differences in pronunciation between the tribes. The Hebrew word shibboleth itself means “stream” or “flood,” and was apparently chosen simply as a test case without regard to its meaning.
notes.765: (tn, Heb): “and could not prepare to speak.” The precise meaning of יָכִין (yakhin) is unclear. Some understand it to mean “was not careful [to say it correctly]”; others emend to יָכֹל (yakhol, “was not able [to say it correctly]”) or יָבִין (yavin, “did not understand [that he should say it correctly]”), which is read by a few Hebrew mss.

rashi.heb:
*אמר נא שבולת.* 
שבולת הנהר הזה אעבור:
rashi.eng: *Say now 'Shibboleth’.* (say) this stream (שִׁבֹּלֶת) of the river will I cross.

rashi.heb:
*ולא יכין לדבר כן.* 
שהיו מגמגמים בלשונם:
rashi.eng: *and he was not prepared to pronounce it properly.* They stumbled in their speech.

notes.767: (tn, Heb): “Jephthah the Gileadite.” The proper name has been replaced by the pronoun (“he”) in the translation for stylistic reasons.
notes.768: (tc): The Hebrew text has “in the cities of Gilead.” The present translation has support from some ancient Greek textual witnesses.

notes.769: (map): For location see Map5-B1; Map7-E2; Map8-E2; Map10-B4.

rashi.heb:
*אבצן.* 
זה בועז:
rashi.eng: *Ibzan.* This was Boaz (who came from Beth-lehem).

notes.771: (tn, Heb): “thirty daughters he sent off outside.” Another option is to translate, “He arranged for his thirty daughters…” It is not clear if he had more than the “thirty daughters” mentioned in the text.
notes.772: (tn, Heb): “and thirty daughters he brought for his sons from the outside.”
notes.773: (tn, Heb): “He”; the referent (Ibzan) has been specified in the translation for clarity and for English stylistic reasons.

notes.775: (tn, Heb): “Ibzan.” The pronoun “he” is used in the translation in keeping with English style, which tends to use a proper name first in a sentence followed by a pronoun rather than vice versa.

notes.777: (tn, Heb): “…led Israel. He led Israel for ten years.”

notes.781: (tn): The adjective “angelic” is interpretive (also in vv. 6, 9).

notes.784: (tn, Heb): “eat anything unclean.” Certain foods were regarded as ritually “unclean” (see Lev 11). Eating such food made one ritually “contaminated.”

rashi.heb:
*יין ושכר.* 
(תרגום:) חמר חדת ועתיק:
rashi.eng: *wine or strong drink.* יַיִן וְשֵׁכָר. New and old wine [after Targum Jonathan].

notes.785: (tn): Another option is to translate, “you are already pregnant and will have a son.” The earlier reference to her being infertile (v. 3) suggests that her conception is still future, but it is possible that the earlier statement only reflects her perspective (as far as she is concerned, she is infertile). According to this interpretation, in v. 5 the angel reveals the truth to her – actually she has recently conceived and is now pregnant (see the translation in R. G. Boling, Judges [AB], 217). Usage favors this interpretation. The predicate adjective הָרָה (harah, “[be/become] pregnant”) elsewhere has a past (1 Sam 4:19) or present (Gen 16:11; 38:25; 2 Sam 11:5) translation value.
