(The usage in Isa 7:14 is debated, but a present translation is definitely possible there.) A final, but less likely possibility, is that she miraculously conceived during the angel’s speech, sometime between his statements recorded in vv. 3 and 5.
notes.786: (tn, Heb): “a razor should not go up on his head.”
notes.787: (tn): Or “set apart to God.” Traditionally the Hebrew term נָזִיר (nazir) has been translated “Nazirite.” The word is derived from the verb נָזַר (nazar, “to dedicate; to consecrate; to set apart”).

rashi.heb:
*ומורה.* 
תער, על שם שמורה ומשליך את השער:
rashi.eng: *וּמוֹרָה.* (Lit., a thrower.) This is a razor because it casts and throws off hair.

notes.790: (tn, Heb): “His appearance was like the appearance of the messenger of God, very awesome.”

notes.791: (tn): See the note on the word “son” in 13:5, where this same statement occurs.
notes.792: (tn, Heb): “eat anything unclean.” Certain foods were regarded as ritually “unclean” (see Lev 11). Eating such food made one ritually “contaminated.”

rashi.heb:
*ואל תאכלי כל טמאה.* 
דברים האסורים לנזיר:
rashi.eng: *and do not eat any unclean (things).* Of those things that are prohibited to a Nazir.

notes.794: (tn): The Hebrew text adds “and said.” This has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.
notes.797: (tc): The LXX has “enlighten,” understanding the Hebrew to read וִיאִירֵנוּ (vi’irenu, “to give light”) rather than the reading of the MT, וְיוֹרֵנוּ (v�yorenu, “to teach”).

rashi.heb:
*לנער היולד.* 
העתיד להוולד:
rashi.eng: *לַנַּעַר הַיּוּלָּד.* To the lad that will be born.

notes.799: (tn, Heb): “God listened to the voice of Manoah.”

notes.801: (tn, Heb): “and said to him.” This phrase has not been translated for stylistic reasons.

rashi.heb:
*אחרי אשתו.* 
אחר עצתה:
rashi.eng: *after his wife.* after her counsel.

notes.808: (tn, Heb): “what will be the child’s rule [i.e., way of life] and his work?”

rashi.heb:
*מה יהיה משפט הנער ומעשהו.* 
(תרגום:) מה חזי למעבד לעולימא ומה נעביד ליה:
rashi.eng: *what shall be the rule for the lad, and his doing.* What is proper for the lad and what shall be done to him [after Targum Jonathan].

notes.810: (tn, Heb): “To everything I said to the woman she should pay attention.” The Hebrew word order emphasizes “to everything,” probably because Manoah’s wife did not tell her husband everything the angel had said to her (cf. vv. 3-5 with v. 7). If she had, Manoah probably would not have been so confused about the child’s mission.

notes.812: (tn, Heb): “eat anything unclean.” Certain foods were regarded as ritually “unclean” (see Lev 11). Eating such food made one ritually “contaminated.”

notes.813: (tn, Heb): “Please allow us to detain you.”
notes.814: (tn, Heb): “so we can prepare before you a young goat of the goats.”

rashi.heb:
*נעצרה נא אותך.* 
נאסוף אותך אל הבית:
rashi.eng: *Let us take you in now.* Let us ingather you into the house.

notes.816: (tn): The words “he said this” are supplied in the translation for clarification. Manoah should have known from these words that the messenger represented the Lord. In the preceding narrative the narrator has informed the reader that the visitor is the Lord’s messenger, but Manoah and his wife did not perceive this. In vv. 5 and 7 the angel refers to “God” (אֱלֹהִים, ’elohim), not the Lord (יְהוַה, y�hvah). Manoah’s wife calls the visitor “a man sent from God” and “God’s messenger” (v. 6), while Manoah prays to the “Lord” (אֲדוֹנָי, ’adonay) and calls the visitor “a man sent from God” (v. 8).

notes.817: (tn, Heb): “Who your name? For [when] your word comes [to pass], we will honor you.” Manoah apparently gets tongue-tied and uses the wrong pronoun (“who” instead of “what”). He starts to say, “Who are you?” But then he switches to “your name” as if he began the sentence with “what.” See R. G. Boling, Judges (AB), 222.

rashi.heb:
*כי יבא דברך.* 
אם יבא לנו שליחות דבר מאתך, משנדע ונכיר את שמך:
rashi.eng: *that when your word will come.* If a message will come from you, by knowing and recognizing your name.

rashi.heb:
*וכבדנוך.* 
ונעשה מה שתשלח לנו:
rashi.eng: *we will honor you.* and do that which you request.

notes.818: (tn, Heb): “Why do you ask for my name, for it is incomprehensible?” The Hebrew adjective פִּלְאִי (pile’iy, “wonderful, incomprehensible”) refers to what is in a category of its own and is beyond full human understanding. Note the use of this word in Ps 139:6, where God’s knowledge is described as incomprehensible and unattainable.

rashi.heb:
*והוא פלאי.* 
מכוסה, תמיד הוא משתנה ואין ידוע למה משתנה היום (ספרי נשא מב):
rashi.eng: *וְהוּא פֶּלִאי.* I.e., hidden. It is constantly changed and it is not known to what it was changed today.

notes.819: (tc, Heb): “Doing an extraordinary deed while Manoah and his wife were watching.” The subject of the participle is missing. The translation assumes that the phrase “the Lord’s messenger” was lost by homoioteleuton. If the text originally read לַיהוָה מַלְאַךְ יְהוָה (layhavah mal’akh y�hvah), the scribe’s eye could have jumped from the first יְהוָה to the second, accidentally omitting two of the three words. Later the conjunction וּ (shureq) would have been added to the following מַפְלִא (mafli’) for syntactical reasons. Another possibility is that a pronominal subject (הוּא, hu’) has been lost in the MT due to haplography.

notes.820: (tn, Heb): “in the flame from the altar.”

notes.822: (tn, Heb): “Then Manoah knew that he was the Lord’s messenger.”

notes.823: (tn): Or “seen God.” Some take the Hebrew term אֱלֹהִים (’elohim) as the divine name (“God”) here, but this seems unlikely since v. 21 informs us that Manoah realized this was the Lord’s messenger, not God himself. Of course, he may be exaggerating for the sake of emphasis. Another option, the one followed in the translation, understands Manoah to be referring to a lesser deity. The term אֱלֹהִים (’elohim) is sometimes used of an individual deity other than the Lord (see BDB 43 s.v. 2.a). One cannot assume that Manoah was a theologically sophisticated monotheist.

rashi.heb:
*וכעת.* 
הזאת:
rashi.eng: *וְכָעֵת.* (Lit., and at a time) I.e., and at this time.

rashi.heb:
*לא השמיענו כזאת.* 
לא היה משמיענו בשורה זו אם ראויים אנו למות:
rashi.eng: *He would not let us hear (such things) as these.* He would not let us hear such news (of our child) if we were deserving of death.

notes.825: (tn, Heb): “the woman.” For clarity this has been specified in the translation as “Manoah’s wife.”
notes.826: (tn): The name appears to mean “sun-like” or “solar.”

notes.828: (tn): Or “move him to action”; or “stir him.”

rashi.heb:
*לפעמו.* 
לבא בקרבו לפעמים:
rashi.eng: *לְפַעֲמוֹ.* To come within him at times (לִפְעָמִים).

notes.829: (tn, Heb): “and he saw a woman in Timnah, one of the daughters of the Philistines.”

notes.831: (tn, Heb): “I have seen a woman in Timnah, one of the daughters of the Philistines.”

notes.832: (tn, Heb): “my.” The singular may seem strange, since the introduction to the quotation attributes the words to his father and mother. But Samson’s father apparently speaks for both himself and his wife. However, the Lucianic recension of the LXX and the Syriac Peshitta have a second person pronoun here (“you”), and this may represent the original reading.
notes.833: (tn, Heb): “Is there not among the daughters of your brothers or among all my people a woman that you have to go to get a wife among the uncircumcised Philistines?”
notes.834: (tn): “Her” is first in the Hebrew word order for emphasis. Samson wanted this Philistine girl, no one else. See C. F. Burney, Judges, 357.
notes.835: (tn, Heb): “because she is right in my eyes.”

notes.837: (tn, Heb): “for an opportunity he was seeking from the Philistines.”

rashi.heb:
*כי תואנה הוא מבקש.* 
עלילה להתגרות בם:
rashi.eng: *that he sought a pretense.* I.e., a pretense to antagonize them.

notes.838: (tc): The MT reads, “Samson went down with his father and mother to Timnah. When they approached…” Verse 6b states that Samson did not tell his parents about his encounter with the lion (vv. 5b-6a), but v. 5a gives the impression they would have seen the entire episode. One could assume that Samson separated from his parents prior to the lion’s attack, but the Hebrew text does not indicate this. It seems more likely that the words “with his father and his mother” were accidentally copied into the text, perhaps under the influence of v. 4a, where the same phrase appears. An original singular verb (“he approached”) may have been changed to the plural form (“they approached”) after the words “his father and his mother” were accidentally added to the text.
notes.839: (tn, Heb): “and look, a young lion of the lions was roaring to meet him.”

notes.841: (tn, Heb): “him” or “it”; the referent (the lion) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
notes.842: (tn, Heb): “and there was nothing in his hand.”

notes.844: (tn, Heb): “She was the right one in the eyes of Samson.”

rashi.heb:
*וידבר לאשה.* 
על האשה, דבר לקרוביה, כן תרגם יונתן:
rashi.eng: *and he talked to the woman (lit.).* I.e., concerning the woman, he spoke to her relatives. So renders Targum Jonathan .

notes.846: (tn, Heb): “and look, a swarm of bees…”

rashi.heb:
*עדת דבורים.* 
(תרגום:) קינא דדברייתא, כניסת דבורים:
rashi.eng: *עֲדַת דְּבוֹרִים.* (Targum Jonathan renders) דְּדַבַּרְיָתָא קִינָא, a swarm of bees.

notes.847: (tn, Heb): “went.” Samson apparently went home to his parents before going to Timnah for the marriage. Seeing and tasting the honey appears to encourage Manoah to go with his son to Timnah. Perhaps both Samson and his father viewed the honey as a good omen of future blessing. Possibly Samson considered it a symbol of sexual pleasure or an aphrodisiac. Note the use of honey imagery in Song 4:11 and 5:1.
notes.848: (sn): Touching the carcass of a dead animal undoubtedly violated Samson’s Nazirite status. See Num 6:6.

rashi.heb:
*וירדהו.* 
לשון הבדלת דיבוק של כל דבר הנדבק, וכן לענין פת הנדבקת בתנור, נקראת הבדלתו רדייה, (שבת קיז ב): הרודה פת מן התנור, (בבא מציעא סד א): הרודה את כוורתו, על שם שהדבש עשוי על ידי חלות שעושה מדובק בדופני הכלי בכל צדדין מדופן אל דופן, כמדת עוגל הכלי, וכן תרגם יונתן: וירדהו, ונסחיה:
rashi.eng: *וַיִּרְדֵּהוּ.* This is an expression of separating anything which is clinging, as by bread clinging to an oven, its removal is called רְדִיָּה (Sab. 117b) “One who separates (הָרוֹדֶה) bread from an oven,” (ibid. 95a) “One who separates (הָרוֹדֶה) from his hive,” since the honey is contained in honeycombs clinging to the walls of the vessel on all sides from wall to wall according to the circumference of the vessel. Likewise Targum Jonathan renders וַיִּרְדֵּהוּ as וְנַסְחֵיהּ (and he separated).

notes.849: (tn, Heb): “And his father went down to the woman.”

rashi.heb:
*וירד אביהו אל האשה.* 
(תרגום:) על עסקי איתתא:
rashi.eng: *Now his father went down to the woman (lit.).* I.e., concerning the woman [after Targum Jonathan].

notes.852: (tn, Heb): “When they saw him, they gave him thirty companions and they were with him.” Instead of כִּרְאוֹתָם (kir’otam, “when they saw”) some ancient witnesses (e.g., some mss of the LXX) assume the reading בְּיִרְאָתָם (b�yir’atam, “because they feared”).

rashi.heb:
*מרעים.* 
חברים לשושבינות:
rashi.eng: *מֵרֵעִים.* companions.

notes.853: (tn, Heb): “If you really can tell it to me [during] the seven days of the feast and you find [its answer].”

notes.855: (tn, Heb): “you are unable to tell me.”
notes.856: (tn, Heb): “Give your riddle so we can hear it.”

notes.857: (tc): The MT reads “seventh.” In Hebrew there is a difference of only one letter between the words רְבִיעִי (r�vi’i, “fourth”) and שְׁבִיעִי (sh�vi’i, “seventh”). Some ancient textual witnesses (e.g., LXX and the Syriac Peshitta) read “fourth,” here, which certainly harmonizes better with the preceding verse (cf. “for three days”) and with v. 17. Another option is to change שְׁלֹשֶׁת (sh�loshet, “three”) at the end of v. 14 to שֵׁשֶׁת (sheshet, “six”), but the resulting scenario does not account as well for v. 17, which implies the bride had been hounding Samson for more than one day.
notes.858: (tn, Heb): “Entice your husband so that he might tell us the riddle.”
notes.860: (tn): The Hebrew text expands the statement: “burn up with fire.” The words “with fire” are redundant in English and have been omitted from the translation for stylistic reasons.
notes.862: (tc): The translation assumes the Hebrew form הֲלֹם (halom, “here,” attested in five Hebrew mss and supported by the Targum), instead of the inexplicable הֲלֹא (halo’), a negative particle with interrogative particle prefixed to it.
notes.863: (tn): For discussion of this difficult form, see C. F. Burney, Judges, 364.

rashi.heb:
*ויהי ביום השביעי.* 
לימות השבת, ולא שביעי למשתה, והוא רביעי לימי המשתה:
rashi.eng: *And it was, on the seventh day.* Of the week, not the seventh (day) of the feasting but rather the fourth day of feasting.

rashi.heb:
*הלירשנו קראתם לנו הלא.* 
תרגם יונתן: הלמסכנותנא קריתון יתנא הלכא:
rashi.eng: *have you called us here to impoverish us.* Targum Jonathan renders: Have you called us here (הֲלֹא = הֲלוֹם) to impoverish us?

notes.869: (tn, Heb): “the seven days [during] which they held the party.” This does not mean she cried for the entire seven days; v. 15 indicates otherwise. She cried for the remainder of the seven day period, beginning on the fourth day.
notes.871: (tn, Heb): “she told the riddle to the sons of her people.”

rashi.heb:
*שבעת הימים.* 
הנותרים משבעת הימים, מרביעי ואילך:
rashi.eng: *the seven days.* I.e., the remainder of the seven days, from the fourth and onward.

notes.872: (sn): Plowed with my heifer. This statement emphasizes that the Philistines had utilized a source of information which should have been off-limits to them. Heifers were used in plowing (Hos 10:11), but one typically used one’s own farm animals, not another man’s.

rashi.heb:
*בטרם יבא החרסה.* 
לפני שקיעת החמה, שעדיין היה להם שהות עד הערב:
rashi.eng: *before the sun set.* Before sunset, since they still had time until evening.

rashi.heb:
*חרשתם בעגלתי.* 
משל הוא (תרגום:) אילולפון בדקתון באתתי:
rashi.eng: *plowed with my heifer.* This is allegorical (as Targum Jonathan renders): “Had you not interrogated my wife.”

notes.875: (tn, Heb): “he went up to his father’s house.”

rashi.heb:
*רוח ה'.* 
(תרגום:) רוח גבורה מן קדם ה':
rashi.eng: *a spirit of the Lord.* A spirit of might emanating from God (Targum Jonathan).

rashi.heb:
*חליצותם.* 
מלבושים שחלץ מעליהן:
rashi.eng: *clothing.* I. e., the clothing that he removed (שֶחָלַץ has similar construction) from them.

notes.876: (tn, Heb): “to his companion who had been his attendant.”

rashi.heb:
*למרעהו.* 
לאחד משושביניו נתנה:
rashi.eng: *לְמֵרֵעֵהוּ אֲשֶׁר רֵעָה לוֹ.* She was given to one of his companions.

notes.877: (sn): The wheat harvest took place during the month of May. See O. Borowski, Agriculture in Iron Age Israel, 37, 88.
notes.878: (tn, Heb): “Samson visited his wife with a young goat.”
notes.879: (tn): The words “to her father” are supplied in the translation (see the end of the verse).
notes.880: (tn, Heb): “I will go to my wife in the bedroom.” The Hebrew idiom בּוֹא אֶל (bo’ ’el, “to go to”) often has sexual connotations. The cohortative form used by Samson can be translated as indicating resolve (“I want to go”) or request (“let me go”).

notes.881: (tn, Heb): “saying, I said.” The first person form of אָמַר (’amar, “to say”) sometimes indicates self-reflection. The girl’s father uses the infinitive absolute for emphasis.
notes.882: (tn, Heb): “hating, you hated.” Once again the girl’s father uses the infinitive absolute for emphasis.
notes.883: (tn, Heb): “Is her younger sister not better than her? Let her [i.e., the younger sister] be yours instead of her [i.e., Samson’s ‘bride’]).”

notes.884: (tc): Codex Alexandrinus (A) of the (original) LXX has the singular “to him.”
notes.885: (tn, Heb): “I am innocent this time from the Philistines when I do with them harm.”

rashi.heb:
*נקיתי הפעם.* 
בדין אעשה להם הרעה:
rashi.eng: *This time I shall be blameless.* Justly will I harm them.

notes.887: (tn, Heb): “He turned tail to tail and placed one torch between the two tails in the middle.”

rashi.heb:
*ויפן.* 
את הזנבות זנב אל זנב ויפן, משמע הוא עצמו פנה (שמות לב טו) ;. ויפן, משמע הפנה את אחרים, וכן שימוש כל תיבה שפעל שלה בה"א ; (שמות א כ): וירב העם ; (איכה ב ה): וירב בבת יהודה תאניה ; (מלכים ב כה כא): ויגל יהודה מעל אדמתו, הגלה ; (שם ב: יח יא): ויגל מלך אשור את ישראל אשורה, ויגלה:
rashi.eng: *and turned.* The tails, tail to tail. וַיִּפֶן implies he himself turned. וַיַּפֶן implies he made others turn. And likewise is conjugated every word whose verb contains a “heh” (at the end which drops such as גלה רבה פנה) as in, (Ex. 1:20) הָעָם וַיִּרֶב (“And the people multiplied”), (Lamen. 2:5) יְהוּדָה וַיֶרֶב בְּבַת (“And He multiplied in Judah grief”), (II Kings 25:21) וַיִּגֶל יְהוּדָה מֵעַל אַדְמָתוֹ (“And Judah exited from his land”), (II Kings 17:6) וַיֶּגֶל אֶת ישְׂרָאֵל אַשּׁוּרָה (“And he exiled Israel to Ashur”) [as per Shem Ephraim].

rashi.heb:
*חתן התמני.* 
חתן הפלשתי אשר בתמנה (לעיל יד א):
rashi.eng: *the son-in-law of the Timnite.* The son-in-law of the Philistine who is in Timnah.

notes.894: (tn): The Niphal of נָקָם (naqam, “to avenge, to take vengeance”) followed by the preposition ב (bet) has the force “to get revenge against.” See 1 Sam 18:25; Jer 50:15; Ezek 25:12.

rashi.heb:
*אם תעשון כזאת.* 
ושמא רגילין אתם בכך, לתת אשתו של זה לזה:
rashi.eng: *Are you accustomed to do like this.* Perhaps you are accustomed to do such; to give the wife of one to another?

notes.896: (tn, Heb): “He struck them, calf on thigh, [with] a great slaughter.” The precise meaning of the phrase “calf on thigh” is uncertain.

rashi.heb:
*שוק על ירך.* 
(תרגום:) פרשין עם רגלאין, רוכב סוס אינו נשען על ירכו כי אם על שוקו, רגל אחד נתון בברזל התלוי במרכבת:
rashi.eng: *the riders and the foot soldiers.* (Lit., leg on thigh) (Targum Jonathan renders) “riders and foot soldiers.” A horse rider is not supported by his thigh but rather by his leg, with one foot inserted into the metal (stirrup) which hangs from the saddle.

rashi.heb:
*בסעיף.* 
בנקרת סלע עיטם, וחברו (ישעיהו נז ה): סעיפי הסלעים, (שם י לג): מסעף פארה:
rashi.eng: *in the cleft .* In the cleft (which is a crevice between the protrusions) of the rock of Etam, and similarly, (Isa. 2:21) וּבִסְעִיפֵי הַסְּלָעִים (“The protrusions of the rocks”), (Isa. 10: 33) מְסָעֵף פֻּארָה (“Will cut down its branches”).

notes.898: (tn): Or “spread out.” The Niphal of נָטָשׁ (natash) has this same sense in 2 Sam 5:18, 22.

rashi.heb:
*וינטשו.* 
ויתפזרו:
rashi.eng: *and spread out.*

rashi.heb:
*בלחי.* 
שם מקום:
rashi.eng: *in Lehi.* (lit., a jaw) This is the name of a place.

notes.900: (tn, Heb): “they”; the referent (the Philistines) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

rashi.heb:
*למה עליתם עלינו.* 
הלא עבדים אנחנו לכם:
rashi.eng: *Why have you come up against us.* Are we not subservient to you?

rashi.heb:
*לאסור את שמשון.* 
שתאסרוהו ותסגירוהו לנו:
rashi.eng: *to bind Samson.* I.e., so that you should bind him and deliver him to us.

notes.902: (tn, Heb): “meet [with hostility]”; “harm.” In light of v. 13, “kill” is an appropriate translation.

notes.903: (tn, Heb): “No,” meaning that they will not harm him.

rashi.heb:
*לא כי אסור נאסרך.* 
לא נהרוג אותך, כי אם אסור נאסרך:
rashi.eng: *No, however we will bind you.* I.e., We will not kill you, however, we will bind you.

rashi.heb:
*רוח ה'.* 
(תרגום:) רוח גבורה מן קדם ה':
rashi.eng: *A spirit of the Lord.* A spirit of might emanating from God [quoting Targum Jonathan].

rashi.heb:
*אסוריו.* 
קשוריו:
rashi.eng: *his bonds .*  His bonds.

notes.908: (tn, Heb): “fresh,” i.e., not decayed and brittle.
notes.909: (tn, Heb): “he reached out his hand and took it.”
notes.910: (tn): The Hebrew text adds “with it.” This has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.

rashi.heb:
*טריה.* 
לחה, וראיתי בספר רפואות שקורא ללחה שיוצא מן המכה: 'טריה':
rashi.eng: *טְרִיָּה.* Moist. I saw in a book of cures that the moisture which issues from a wound is called טְרִיָּה.

notes.911: (tn): The precise meaning of the second half of the line (חֲמוֹר חֲמֹרָתָיִם, khamor khamoratayim) is uncertain. The present translation assumes that the phrase means, “a heap, two heaps” and refers to the heaps of corpses littering the battlefield. Other options include: (a) “I have made donkeys of them” (cf. NIV; see C. F. Burney, Judges, 373, for a discussion of this view, which understands a denominative verb from the noun “donkey”); (b) “I have thoroughly skinned them” (see HALOT 330 s.v. IV cj. חמר, which appeals to an Arabic cognate for support); (c) “I have stormed mightily against them,” which assumes the verb חָמַר (khamar, “to ferment; to foam; to boil up”).

rashi.heb:
*חמור חמרתים.* 
בלחי החמור לצבור צברים רבים, (תרגום:) בלועא דחמרא רמיתינון דגורין:
rashi.eng: *חֲמוֹר חֲמוֹרָתָיִם.* With the jawbone of a donkey I piled many piles, i.e., with the jawbone of a donkey I heaped them up [after Targum Jonathan].

notes.913: (sn): The name Ramath Lehi means “Height of the Jawbone.”

notes.914: (tn, Heb): “you have placed into the hand of your servant.”
notes.915: (tn, Heb): “the uncircumcised,” which in context refers to the Philistines.

notes.916: (tn): The word translated “basin” refers to a circular-shaped depression in the land’s surface.
notes.918: (tn, Heb): “named it”; the referent (the spring) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
notes.919: (sn): The name En Hakkore means “Spring of the one who cries out.”

rashi.heb:
*את המכתש.* 
גומא שהשן יושבת בה, עשויה כעין מכתשת:
rashi.eng: *the socket.* The socket within which the tooth rests, thich is shaped like a mortar (מַכְתֶּשֶׁת)

rashi.heb:
*עין הקורא.* 
מעין שבא על ידי זעקת הקורא אל ה':
rashi.eng: *En-hakkore.*  The fountain (מַעְיָן) that came about through the prayers of the one who called (הַקּוֹרֵא) to God.

notes.921: (tn, Heb): “in the days of the Philistines.”

notes.922: (tn, Heb): “and he went in to her.” The idiom בּוֹא אֶל (bo’ ’el, “to go to”) often has sexual connotations.

notes.923: (tc, Heb): “To the Gazites, saying.” A verb is missing from the MT; some ancient Greek witnesses add “it was reported.”
notes.924: (tn, Heb): “And they surrounded.” The rest of the verse suggests that “the town” is the object, not “the house.” Though the Gazites knew Samson was in the town, apparently they did not know exactly where he had gone. Otherwise, they would could have just gone into or surrounded the house and would not have needed to post guards at the city gate.
notes.925: (tn, Heb): “and they lay in wait for him all night in the city gate.”
notes.928: (tn): The words “He will not leave” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
notes.929: (tn, Heb): “until the light of the morning.”

rashi.heb:
*לעזתים לאמר.* 
לאנשי עזה נאמר:
rashi.eng: *To the Gazites, saying (Lit.).* To the people of Gaza it was told.

rashi.heb:
*ויתחרשו.* 
נהגו עצמן בשתיקה:
rashi.eng: *And they were quiet.* They conducted themselves quietly.

notes.930: (tn, Heb): “And Samson lay until the middle of the night and arose in the middle of the night.”
notes.932: (tn, Heb): “which is upon the face of Hebron.”

rashi.heb:
*ויסעם.* 
ויעקרם ממקומם:
rashi.eng: *וַיִּסָּעֵם.* And he uprooted them from their place.

notes.933: (tn, Heb): “subdue him in order to humiliate him.”

notes.934: (tn, Heb): “how you can be subdued in order to be humiliated.”

notes.936: (tn): The word refers to a bowstring, probably made from animal tendons. See Ps 11:2; Job 30:11.

rashi.heb:
*יתרים.* 
חבלים דקים:
rashi.eng: *bowstrings.* I.e., thin cords.

notes.937: (tn, Heb): “And the ones lying in wait were sitting for her.” The grammatically singular form וְהָאֹרֵב (v�ha’orev) is collective here, referring to the rulers as a group (so also in v. 16).

rashi.heb:
*ולא נודע כחו.* 
לא הוצרך להתחזק בנתקו אותם:
rashi.eng: *and his strength was not known.* He did not have to exert himself to tear them.

notes.941: (tn): See Gen 31:7; Exod 8:29 [8:25 HT]; Job 13:9; Isa 44:20; Jer 9:4 for other uses of this Hebrew word (II תָּלַל, talal), which also occurs in v. 13.

notes.942: (tn, Heb): “with which no work has been done.”

rashi.heb:
*בעבותים.* 
חבלים גסים:
rashi.eng: *ropes.* I.e., thick cords.

notes.944: (tn, Heb): “And the ones lying in wait were sitting in the bedroom.”
notes.945: (tn, Heb): “them”; the referent (the ropes) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

notes.946: (tn, Heb): “head” (also in the following verse). By metonymy the head is mentioned in the Hebrew text in place of the hair on it.
notes.947: (tn, Heb): “with the web.” For a discussion of how Delilah did this, see C. F. Burney, Judges, 381, and G. F. Moore, Judges (ICC), 353-54.

rashi.heb:
*מחלפות.* 
קווצות, פלוני"ש בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *מַחְלְפוֹת.* Locks. Pelous (פלודיש) in O.F.

rashi.heb:
*עם המסכת.* 
עץ שהגרדי מיסך בו את השתי, ושם העץ אנשובל"א מסכת, אורטר"א בלע"ז:
rashi.eng: *to the roller.* The wood upon which the weaver spreads out the warp. The name of this wood is ensouple in O.F. The roller (is called) ourdissuire in O.F.

notes.949: (tc): The MT of vv. 13b-14a reads simply, “He said to her, ‘If you weave the seven braids of my head with the web.’ And she fastened with the pin and said to him.” The additional words in the translation, “and secure it with the pin, I will become weak and be like any other man.’ So she made him go to sleep, wove the seven braids of his hair into the fabric on the loom,” which without doubt represent the original text, are supplied from the ancient Greek version. (In both vv. 13b and 14a the Greek version has “to the wall” after “with the pin,” but this is an interpretive addition that reflects a misunderstanding of ancient weaving equipment. See G. F. Moore, Judges [ICC], 353-54.) The Hebrew textual tradition was accidentally shortened during the copying process. A scribe’s eye jumped from the first instance of “with the web” to the second, causing him to leave out inadvertently the intervening words.
notes.950: (tn): The Hebrew adds, “from his sleep.” This has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.

notes.951: (tn, Heb): “when your heart is not with me.”

notes.953: (tn, Heb): “and his spirit was short [i.e., impatient] to the point of death.”

rashi.heb:
*ותאלצהו.* 
דחקתו, ואין לו דמיון:
rashi.eng: *וַתְּאַלְצֵהוּ.* And she pressed him.

notes.955: (tn, Heb): “a razor has not come upon my head.”
notes.956: (tn): Or “set apart to God.” Traditionally the Hebrew term נָזִיר (nazir) has been translated “Nazirite.” The word is derived from the verb נָזַר (nazar, “to dedicate; to consecrate; to set apart”).
notes.957: (tn, Heb): “from the womb of my mother.”
notes.958: (tn, Heb): “I.” The referent has been made more specific in the translation (“my head”).

notes.961: (tc): The translation follows the Qere, לִי (li, “to me”) rather than the Kethib, לָהּ (lah, “to her”).

rashi.heb:
*ותרא דלילה כי הגיד לה.* 
ניכרין דברי אמת:
rashi.eng: *And Delilah saw that he had told her.* The words of truth are discernable.

notes.963: (tn, Heb): “on her knees.” The expression is probably euphemistic for sexual intercourse. See HALOT 160-61 s.v. בֶּרֶךְ.
notes.964: (tn, Heb): “she called for a man and she shaved off.” The point seems to be that Delilah acted through the instrumentality of the man. See J. A. Soggin, Judges (OTL), 254.
notes.965: (tn, Heb): “head.” By metonymy the hair of his head is meant.
notes.966: (tn, Heb): “She began to humiliate him.” Rather than referring to some specific insulting action on Delilah’s part after Samson’s hair was shaved off, this statement probably means that she, through the devious actions just described, began the process of Samson’s humiliation which culminates in the following verses.

rashi.heb:
*ותקרא לאיש.* 
לשלוחן של סרנים:
rashi.eng: *and she called to the man.* To the messenger of the lords.

notes.968: (tn): The Hebrew adds, “from his sleep.” This has not been included in the translation for stylistic reasons.
notes.970: (tn, Heb): “I will go out as before.”

rashi.heb:
*ויורידו אותו עזתה.* 
מקום תחלת קלקולו:
rashi.eng: *And they brought him down to Gaza.* (This was) the location of his first corruption (above v. 1).

rashi.heb:
*ויהי טוחן.* 
בריחים, מלאכה כבדה ורבותינו (סוטה י א) פירשו מה שפירשו:
rashi.eng: *and he did grind.* With a mill. This was hard labor. However, our Sages explained that which they explained.

notes.972: (tn): Most interpret this as a reference to Samson, but this seems premature, since v. 25 suggests he was not yet standing before them. Consequently some prefer to see this statement as displaced and move it to v. 25 (see C. F. Burney, Judges, 387). It seems more likely that the pronoun refers to an image of Dagon.

rashi.heb:
*בין העמודים.* 
אשר הבית נכון עליהם:
rashi.eng: *between the pillars.* Upon which the building was supported.

notes.976: (tn, Heb): “the pillars upon which the house is founded.”

rashi.heb:
*והמישני.* 
פאלפא"ר בלע"ז, כמו (בראשית כז יב): אולי ימושני:
rashi.eng: *and let me feel.* Heb. וַהֲמִישֵנִי, Palpare (פלפאר) in O.F. as in, (Gen. 27: 12) “Perhaps my father will feel me” (יְמֻשֵּׁנִי).

notes.978: (tn): The Hebrew has אֲדֹנָי יֱהֹוִה (’adonay yehovih, “Lord Yahweh”).
notes.979: (tn, Heb): “so I can get revenge with one act of vengeance.”

rashi.heb:
*זכרני נא.* 
זכור עשרים שנה ששפטתי את ישראל, ולא אמרתי לאחד מהם העבר לי מקל זה ממקום למקום:
rashi.eng: *remember me.* Remember the twenty years that I judged Israel and did not tell one of them “Move this stick for me from one place to another.”

rashi.heb:
*נקם אחת משתי עיני.* 
ושכר עין השנית הנח לי לעולם הבא, וכאן פרע לי שכר אחת מהן:
rashi.eng: *the vengeance for one of my two eyes.* And the reward for the second eye reserve for me for the world to come, but here pay me the reward for one of them.

notes.980: (tn, Heb): “the pillars upon which the house was founded.”

rashi.heb:
*וילפת.* 
ויאחז, אינברצ"א בלע"ז, כמו (רות ג ח): ויחרד האיש וילפת, נאחז בזרועות האשה:
rashi.eng: *וַיִּלְפֹּת.* And he grasped. Embrasser (אינברצא) in O.F. as in, (Ruth 3: 8) “And the man trembled and was grasped” (וַיִּלָּפֵת), he was grasped by the arms of the woman.

notes.982: (tn, Heb): “And the ones whom he killed in his death were many more than he killed in his life.”

notes.983: (tn, Heb): “and all the house of his father.”
notes.984: (tn, Heb): “and lifted him up and brought up.”

rashi.heb:
*ויהי איש מהר אפרים.* 
אף על פי שנכתבו שתי פרשיות הללו בסוף הספר, של מיכה ושל פלגש בגבעה, בתחלת השופטים היה, בימי עתניאל בן קנז, שנאמר (לקמן יח לא): וישימו להם את פסל מיכה וגו' כל ימי היות בית אלהים בשילה, למדנו שכל ימי שילה היה דמות של מיכה, ובפלגש בגבעה נאמר על יבוס שבירושלים (שם יט יב): לא נסור אל עיר נכרי, למדנו שעדיין לא כבשו את ירושלים:
rashi.eng: *Now there was a man from the mountain of Ephraim.* Although the following two episodes are written at the end of this book; the one of Micah and the other about the concubine of Gibeah, they, nevertheless, occurred at the beginning of the period of the Judges. This was during the days of Othniel the son of Kenaz (and Cushan, above 3:8 11) as it says, (below 18:31) “And they accepted for themselves the graven image of Micah which he had made, throughout the period that the house of God was in Shiloh,” so we can derive that for the duration of Shiloh (Fourteen years after Israel’s crossing the Jordan, the Tabernacle was erected in Shiloh and remained there for three hundred sixty-nine years.) the image of Micah remained. Also, by the concubine of Gibeah it is said concerning the Jebusites of Jerusalem, (below 19:12) “We will not turn into (this) city of heathens,” so we can derive that they had not yet captured Jerusalem (which was captured by Judah, see above 1:8).

notes.986: (tn): The words “You know” are supplied in the translation for clarification.
notes.989: (tn): In the Hebrew text the statement, “but now I am giving it back to you,” appears at the end of v. 3 and is spoken by the mother. But v. 4 indicates that she did not give the money back to her son. Unless the statement is spoken by the woman to the LORD, it appears to be misplaced and fits much better in v. 2. It may have been accidentally omitted from a manuscript, written in the margin, and then later inserted in the wrong place in another manuscript.

rashi.heb:
*אשר לקח לך.* 
אשר נגנב ממך, ויש לו דומה (שמואל א כא ו): כי אשה עצורה לנו, עצורה ממנו:
rashi.eng: *that was taken to you.* Heb. לָ. (Lit.) I.e., that was stolen from you (מִמּ). There is a similar verse: (I Sam. 21:6) “But women are withheld from us” (לָנוּ as מִמֶּנּוּ).

rashi.heb:
*ואת אלית.* 
קללת כל מי שגנבו, וגם אמרת הקללה באזני:
rashi.eng: *and (about which) you did curse.* Anyone who stole it, and you also said the curse in my ears.

rashi.heb:
*הנה הכסף.* 
אני מודה לך עליו שהוא בידי שאני לקחתיו:
rashi.eng: *Behold the silver.* I admit that it is in my possession because I took it.

notes.991: (tn, Heb): “dedicating, I dedicate.” In this case the emphatic infinitive absolute lends a mood of solemnity to the statement.
notes.992: (tn, Heb): “to the LORD from my hand for my son to make a carved image and cast metal image.” She cannot mean that she is now taking the money from her hand and giving it back to her son so he can make an image. Verses 4-6 indicate she took back the money and used a portion of it to hire a silversmith to make an idol for her son to use. The phrase “a carved image and cast metal image” is best taken as referring to two idols (see 18:17-18), even though the verb at the end of v. 4, וַיְהִי (vay�hi, “and it was [in the house of Micah]”), is singular.

rashi.heb:
*וישב את אלף ומאה הכסף לאמו.* 
אמר להחזירו לה, ובמקום שהוא שם הרי הוא ברשותך:
rashi.eng: *And he restored the eleven hundred pieces of silver to his mother.* He said he would return them to her, and wherever they were they would be in her domain.

rashi.heb:
*הקדש הקדשתי את הכסף מידי לבני.* 
קבלתי עלי למסרו מידי לידך לשם דמות ומסכה, תנהו לי עתה ומידי אני אשיבנו אליך יש אומרים שהאשה הזאת היא דלילה, לפי שכתוב (לעיל טז ה): אלף ומאה כסף, וטעות הוא בידם, שהרבה שנים קדם מיכה לשמשון, אך הפרשיות נסמכו על הכסף הרע ששוה כאן וכאן, וכסף של פורענות היו שניהם:
rashi.eng: *I have dedicated the silver (before the Lord) from my hand for my son.* I accepted upon myself to transfer them from my possession to your possession for the purpose of a form and a molten image. Give them to me now, and then, from (being in) my possession I will return them to you. Some say that this woman was Delilah because it mentions eleven hundred pieces of silver (as above 16:5), but they are mistaken because Micah preceded Samson many years. notes.1232: (sn): The number given here (twenty-five thousand sword-wielding Benjaminites) is an approximate figure; v. 35 gives the more exact number (25,100). According to v. 15, the Benjaminite army numbered 26,700 (26,000 + 700). The figures in vv. 35 (rounded in vv. 44-46) and 47 add up to 25,700. What happened to the other 1,000 men? The most reasonable explanation is that they were killed during the first two days of fighting. G. F. Moore (Judges [ICC], 429) and C. F. Burney (Judges, 475) reject this proposal, arguing that the narrator is too precise and concerned about details to omit such a fact. However, the account of the first two days’ fighting emphasizes Israel’s humiliating defeat. To speak of Benjaminite casualties would diminish the literary effect. In vv. 35, 44-47 the narrator’s emphasis is the devastating defeat that Benjamin experienced on this final day of battle. To mention the earlier days’ casualties at this point is irrelevant to his literary purpose. He allows readers who happen to be concerned with such details to draw conclusions for themselves.

rashi.heb:
*ועד בהמה.* 
ואנשים בכלל 'מתום' היו, ש'מתום' לשון כליה הוא ויש לתמוה על אלף היכן הם, שהרי עשרים וששה אלף התפקדו מן הערים, ומן הגבעה שש מאות, וכאן מנה בנופלים עשרים וחמשה אלף ומאה איש, ושש מאות נמלטו אל סלע הרמון, והאלף ברחו אל הערים ונפלו למחרת כששבו בני ישראל אל ערי בנימין להחרים הנשים והטף:
rashi.eng: *even the cattle.* Thus people are included in “destroying” since “מְתֹם” is an expression of destruction. There is a difficulty concerning the whereabouts of a thousand since twenty-six thousand were numbered from the cities and from Gibeah seven (text amended) hundred (v. 15). However, here the count of the fallen is twenty-five thousand and one hundred (v. 35) plus the six hundred that escaped to the rock of Rimmon. But perhaps (amended) the (undermined) thousand fled to the cities and fell the following day when the children of Israel returned to the Benjamite cities to destroy the women and children (as is stated in this verse).

notes.1272: (tn, Heb): “for we did not take each his wife in battle.” Through battle. This probably refers to the battle against Jabesh Gilead, which only produced four hundred of the six hundred wives needed.
notes.1273: (tn): This sentence is not in the Hebrew text. It is supplied in the translation to clarify the logic of the statement.
notes.1274: (tc, Heb): “You did not give to them, now you are guilty.” The MT as it stands makes little sense. It is preferable to emend לֹא (lo’, “not”) to לוּא (lu’, “if”). This particle introduces a purely hypothetical condition, “If you had given to them [but you didn’t].” See G. F. Moore, Judges (ICC), 453-54.

rashi.heb:
*לריב אלינו.* 
ללכת אלינו במלחמה:
rashi.eng: *to quarrel with us.* to go against us in battle.

rashi.heb:
*ואמרנו אליהם חנונו אותם.* 
רחמנו עליהם כי אינם יודעים מה לעשות, 'כי לא לקחנו איש אשתו במלחמה' של יבש גלעד אלא לארבע מאות איש מהם, ואם על השבועה אתם מקפידים, לא עון לכם בדבר 'כי לא אתם נתתם להם' את בנותיכם שתהא לכם אשמה בדבר ושלום לכם אל תיראו:
rashi.eng: *then we will say to them we took pity on them.* We took pity on them because they do not know what to do, because we did not take for each man his wife in the war with Jabesh-gilead but only for four hundred of their men. And if you are concerned about your oath, (be assured that) you have no sin in this matter, because you did not give them your daughters (cf. above v. 1) that you should be guilty in this, (rather) peace will be with you, do not fear.

notes.1276: (tn, Heb): “And they took wives according to their number from the dancing girls whom they abducted.”

notes.1281: (tn, Heb): “Each was doing what was right in his [own] eyes.” Each man did what he considered to be right. The Book of Judges closes with this note, which summarizes the situation of the Israelite tribes during this period.
